title: 2026 Fall Special Town Meeting Warrant Guidance
text: To: Ashland Elected Officials / Ashland Committee Chairs / Ashland Department Heads / Ashland Citizens From: Ashland Select Board Date: August 5, 2026 RE: 2026 Fall Special Town Meeting Warrant Guidance ___ In preparation for the Fall 2026 Special Town Meeting, Tuesday November 10, 2026, the Select Board has established a timetable for the submission and review of proposed Town Meeting warrant articles. This timetable is an effort to provide residents and taxpayers with the best available information for making informed decisions on article requests for action. Fall 2026 Special Town Meeting Warrant Timetable August 5, 2026 Open the Warrant September 20, 2026 Deadline for Notice of Intent to submit Proposed warrant articles. Proposed articles filed with the Select Board Office. September 20, 2026 – October 6, 2026 Due Diligence Period: Select Board presentations and Discussions Public Hearings September 28, 2026 Deadline for Finalized Proposed Articles October 7, 2026 Select Board vote to close and post the warrant October 27, 2026 Warrant Posted – No later than date November 10, 2026 Special Town Meeting The Select Board reserves the right to re-open the Warrant after it is closed to include new articles that address emergency or unanticipated needs and / or circumstances. Warrant Article Guidelines: The Ashland Select Board has a goal of collegial and cooperative interaction with all Town Boards, Committees and residents, as well as providing an opportunity for all articles to be fully vetted and well documented. This will allow for thoughtful deliberation and informed decision-making for all Town Meeting participants. All (non-citizen petitions) Warrant Articles are to be submitted to the Assistant Town Manager, Katherine Bird at kbird@ashlandmass.com.

DuBois Cover photo by Rob Ackerman, rear cover photo by Richard Ferris 1 Bedford, Massachusetts 2026 Annual Town Meeting Warrant To the Voters The Annual Town Meeting Warrant Report contains the information you need to prepare to vote on all the issues before the Town. We are grateful to our professional staff, as well as our elected and appointed boards and committees, who spend hours each year compiling, reviewing, and finalizing the Warrant to help voters determine the health and direction of our common life together. The articles contained in this Warrant reflect the operational needs and proposals for improvements to Town services for Fiscal Year 2027, based on information furnished to the Select Board, Finance Committee, and Capital Expenditure Committee by Town departments, boards, and committees. For each of the 35 articles in this year’s Warrant, you will see the text of the article, followed by a brief explanation in italics, with recommendations from boards and committees provided as guidelines for your consideration. Many of the articles are familiar, voted every year at Town Meeting: the Consent Article, Bills of Prior Years, Revolving Funds Expenditure Limits, and Salary Administration Plan Classification & Wage Schedule, to name just a few. Other articles provide voters with new opportunities to address important and emerging needs in our community. Several prominent articles are summarized below: Article 5 – Shawsheen Technical High School Feasibility Study: Voters will decide whether Bedford should contribute its share toward a feasibility study that could lead to state funding for renovating or rebuilding Shawsheen Valley Technical High School. Article 6 – Community Preservation Budget: This article funds $2.5 million in Community Preservation projects, including improvements to the Town Common, affordable housing support, historic preservation efforts, and recreation upgrades across Bedford. Article 7-8 – Capital Projects Plan: Town Meeting will consider approving over $6,785,700 million in capital investments for infrastructure, including water main upgrades, drainage repairs, school facility improvements, and technology replacements. Article 22-29 – Charter & Bylaw Updates: These articles propose technical updates and clarifications to the Town Charter and General Bylaws to improve consistency, modernize language, and reflect current governance practices. Please bring this booklet with you to Town Meeting, to refer to each article as it is presented and voted on. We are grateful for your continued commitment to Bedford, and we look forward to seeing you at Town Meeting. To learn about accessibility features available at Town Meeting, including accessible seating, printable materials, and microphone access, please visit: https://www.bedfordma.gov/295/Town-Meeting. Paul Mortenson Chair of the Select Board 2 Bedford, Massachusetts 2026 Annual Town Meeting Warrant Finance Committee Report The Finance Committee presents for your approval the Fiscal Year 2027 operating budget that supports the excellent quality of life we enjoy in Bedford. It is based on sound financial planning and careful review of departmental requests. The Finance Committee, Town boards, committees and departments have attempted to find the appropriate balance between minimizing tax increases while maintaining the Town’s historically sound financial position. We continue to strive for a robust and stable financial condition for FY2027 and the future. The Finance Committee began work on the operating budget in the fall, by first considering the available sources of revenue. Some of those sources were: • Certified Free Cash from Fiscal Year 2026 was $15,773,809. Our policy is to leave approximately 50% of free cash to mitigate uncertainty in estimates for various budget items including, but not limited to, local receipts and State Aid. This year we are leaving $7,886,905, which is slightly below target or -53.4%. This year, we recommend using $11,629,719 in FY2026 and $8,419,567 to reduce the FY2027 tax levy. • $1,924,202 is estimated from Payments in Lieu of Taxes (PILOT). • Currently, we are projecting a net increase of $10,252,135 of State Aid, which is an increase of 2.44% from FY26. As a starting point for each Town department and board, the Finance Committee determined initial budget guidelines by allocating available revenue based on a five-year average. This year, the Finance Committee recommended a guideline increase of 2.5% for the School Department and 2.5% for the Select Board, Board of Health, Library and Planning Board budgets over FY2026. We developed the final operating budget accommodating several changes justified by the departments and other known items, which included: • The Select Board budget increased 2.50%, or $614,075 overall from FY2026. This is in line with the 2.5% guideline increase of $614,075 while also maintaining the outstanding services provided to the community. • The Non-Discretionary budgets increased by $1,824,161, or 4.16%, from FY2026, primarily due to health insurance increase of 9.58%. Respectfully submitted, Ben Thomas, Chair Phil Prince, Vice Chair Karen Dunn, Clerk Mark Bailey Allen Jimerson George Lee Tom Rowan Vincent Xu 5 Bedford, Massachusetts Introduction 2026 Annual Town Meeting Warrant Capital Expenditure Committee Report Introduction The Capital Expenditure Committee (CapEx) reviews all requests for funding for major equipment purchases and capital projects submitted by Town and School departments. After careful review, the Committee makes recommendations on which projects should be funded. These projects and their proposed costs are presented in Article 7 – Fiscal Year 2027 Capital Projects Plan (Free Cash) and Article 8- Fiscal Yar Capital Projects Plan (Bonding) in the Annual Town Meeting Warrant. Definition of Capital CapEx defines a capital expenditure as any item or project expenditure of $5,000 or more with a useful life of two or more years. Individual capital items of less than $5,000 each are considered operating expenses and are funded through departmental operating budgets with the exception of multiple, similar items that are “bundled” together to reach an amount that exceeds $30,000. Capital Projects Plan As in prior years, the Assistant Town Manager met regularly with Department Heads over the summer to identify and prioritize capital funding needs for the upcoming fiscal year and future years. In the fall, the Assistant Town Manager and Department Heads met with CapEx on several occasions to review and discuss the proposed capital requests in detail. Each project addresses important needs related to the Town’s facilities, infrastructure, and services. The proposed FY27 capital budget recommends funding just over $6.7 million in capital investments. These include, among others: continuing routine replacements of town vehicles, including replacement of an ambulance; continued investment in School and Town information technology systems and safety-related equipment; stormwater and culvert repairs; ongoing water quality initiatives; and continued improvements to school grounds and pedestrian and roadway safety. The capital budget presented to Town Meeting reflects months of analysis and collaboration, and demonstrates the Town’s commitment to transparency, accountability, and sound financial planning. CapEx makes recommendations on the projects themselves, and funding sources are determined separately. Projects 27-01 through 27-21, totaling $5,604,450 are proposed to be funded through free cash. Projects 2722 through 27-24, totaling $1,181,250 are proposed to be bonded. text: OFFICE OF THE SELECT BOARD The Finnerty House One South Main Street, Post Office Box 670 Belchertown, Massachusetts 01007-0670 Telephone: (413) 323-0403 • Facsimile: (413) 323-0494 WARRANT FOR ANNUAL TOWN MEETING May 11, 2026 Commonwealth of Massachusetts Hampshire, ss. GREETING: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby required to notify and warn all the Inhabitants of the Town of Belchertown, qualified to vote in elections of Town officers, to meet at the polling places in said Belchertown, designated by the Select Board, to wit: IN PRECINCTS A, B, C AND D at Belchertown High School gymnasium, 142 Springfield Road, Belchertown, Massachusetts, on Monday, the 18th day of May A.D. 2026, at eight o’clock in the forenoon, then and there to give in their votes on one ballot to precinct officers of the several polling precincts of said Town for the following officers, to wit: One (1) Board of Assessors member for three (3) years; One (1) Board of Assessors member for two (2) years; Two (2) Board of Health member for three (3) years; One (1) Housing Authority member for four (4) years; One (1) Moderator for three (3) years; One (1) Planning Board member for five (5) years; Two (2) School Committee members for three (3) years each and One (1) Select Board member for three (3) years. The polls will open at eight o’clock in the forenoon and close at eight o’clock in the evening. And you are further required to notify and warn all the Inhabitants of said Belchertown, qualified to vote in Town affairs to meet at the Belchertown High School auditorium at 142 Springfield Road in said Belchertown, on Monday, the 11th day of May, A.D. 2026, at 7:00 p.m., then and there to act on the following articles, viz: The text in red is explanatory text for each article. It is not part of the official article and its purpose is to provide more context. This text was written by the Town Manager or the person/department that submitted the article for the Select Board to use in reviewing the articles. It is included here to help our residents when they are making their decisions on how to vote at Town Meeting. Annual House-Keeping Articles Article 1 To choose the following named officers by nomination: Two (2) Almoners of the Whiting Street and Mrs. Susan M.D. Bridgman Funds, each for one (1) year; and one (1) Trustee of the Calvin Bridgman Fund for three (3) years. Annual Town Meeting Warrant – May 11, 2026 CORRECTED 2026.05.01 1 Trust Funds, first established in 1888, with almoners to be voted at ATM: 1. Calvin Bridgman High School Fund. Income to be used in support of a high school. 2. Calvin Bridgman Library Fund. Income to be used in support of the public library. 3. Whiting Street Fund. Income to be used for “relief and comfort of worthy poor in Belchertown.” 4. Susan M D Bridgman Poor Fund. Income to benefit the “worthy poor,” inhabitant in Belchertown, with a percentage of prior year interest to be paid to the library each year. Article 2 To hear reports of the Officers of the Town and any Committees that may have been appointed by the Town and act thereon. Approval of this article is necessary to finalize the Annual Town Report, as prepared by all Town Departments, Committees, Boards, and Commissions. This year, the Report is available for download and only a limited number of copies will be printed for distribution upon request. Article 3 To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Board of Assessors to appoint themselves to work in their various departments for the ensuing fiscal year, at hourly rates not exceeding the following: • Board of Assessors: $17.50 or take any other action relative thereto. The approval of this article allows the members of the Board of Assessors to be compensated for work conducted in their official capacity, primarily for site visits and inspections. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Article 4 To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or appropriate from available funds in the treasury a sum of money to be used by the Board of Assessors for legal counsel in resolving court tax cases, or take any other action relative thereto. This article authorizes funds to serve as a placeholder for Board of Assessors legal expenses in resolving court tax cases. Additional funds may be transferred as required. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Article 5 To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, or appropriate a sum of money from free cash in the treasury or any other available fund, for the Reserve Fund for use by the Finance Committee, or take any other action relative thereto. Annual Town Meeting Warrant – May 11, 2026 CORRECTED 2026.05.01 2 The reserve fund is used for unforeseen “emergency” expenses. Departments in need must request and obtain approval from the Finance Committee to access these funds. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Article 6 To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Select Board to apply for and accept funds from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts Highway Improvement Program for use on approved town ways, or take any other action relative thereto. Funds received through the Massachusetts Highway Improvement Program are authorized by M.G.L. Ch. 90. These funds are used to repair local roadways and to purchase road building equipment. Access to these funds must be approved at Town Meeting, and the spending is overseen by the Town Manager. Article 7 To see if the Town will vote to appropriate from the Sale of Cemetery Lots Account a sum of money to the Cemetery Lot Development Account, or take any other action relative thereto. At the conclusion of each Cemetery lot sold, a portion of the proceeds is retained and returned to the Public Works Department’s Cemetery Division to develop additional space in our cemeteries for future burials. The passage of this article allows the DPW access to those funds. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Budget, Capital and Financial Articles Article 8 To see if the Town will vote to fix the salaries and compensation of all elected officers of the Town, as provided for by Section 108 of Chapter 41 of the Massachusetts General Laws, as amended; and to raise and appropriate or appropriate from available funds in the treasury, sums of money as may be deemed necessary to defray expenses estimated for the ensuing fiscal year commencing July 1, 2026, or take any other action relative thereto. Article 8 contains a series of separate motions, each of which represents a different Town Department budget including the School Department and Capital improvement projects. title: Special Town Meeting Enhanced Warrant
text: TOWN OF BELCHERTOWN SELECT BOARD The Finnerty House One South Main Street, Post Office Box 670 Belchertown, Massachusetts 01007-0670 Telephone: (413) 323-0403 • Facsimile: (413) 323-0494 WARRANT FOR SPECIAL TOWN MEETING May 11, 2026 Commonwealth of Massachusetts Hampshire, ss. GREETING: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby required to notify and warn all the Inhabitants of the Town of Belchertown, qualified to vote in town affairs to meet at the Belchertown High School Auditorium at 142 Springfield Road in said Belchertown, on Monday, the 11th day of May, A.D. 2026 at 6:30 p.m. o’clock in the evening, then and there to act on the following articles, viz: The text in red is explanatory text for each article. It is not part of the official article and its purpose is to provide more context. This text was written by the Town Manager or the person/department that submitted the article for the Select Board to use in reviewing the articles. It is included here to help our residents when they are making their decisions on how to vote at Town Meeting. Article 1 To see if the Town will vote to transfer sums of money to and from certain line items for the fiscal year 2026 budget, or take any action relative thereto. At the end of every fiscal year, funds are transferred from accounts with a positive balance to accounts with deficits in order to preserve a balanced budget. State law prohibits this practice, with some exceptions, without the approval of the municipality’s legislative body. This practice is also exclusive to the General Government; the School Committee has statutory authorization to transfer funds between budgets without further approval. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Special Town Meeting Warrant – May 11, 2026 1 Article 2 To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money from certain line items to the Stabilization Fund, or take any action relative thereto. Last October, at a Special Town Meeting, $325,000 was transferred from the Stabilization Fund to the Town and School Department health insurance plans to cover an unexpected increase. Excess funds from these accounts is being transferred to reimburse the stabilization fund. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Article 3 To see if the Town will transfer a sum of money to pay unpaid bills of a prior year, or take any action relative thereto. Massachusetts General Law restricts Municipalities from paying bills from a previous Fiscal Year without approval from the Town’s Legislative Body. An affirmative vote will allow the Town to issue payment to any vendors that were not paid in FY-25. Endorsed by Finance Committee, Voted 4-0-0 Special Town Meeting Warrant – May 11, 2026 2

text: Town of Boxborough Massachusetts OFFICIAL WARRANT SPECIAL TOWN MEETING Monday, March 9, 2026 – 7:00 PM Voter check-in begins at 6:30 PM Blanchard Memorial School Gymnasium 493 Massachusetts Avenue, Boxborough Please bring this Warrant with you to the Special Town Meeting Free On-Site Child Care 6:30–9:00 PM Sign up with QR code on page 3 Special Town Election-Related to Articles 1 and 2 March 17, 2026 7:00 AM – 8:00 PM Town Hall, 29 Middle Road 1 TABLE OF CONTENTS ARTICLE 1 PURCHASE OF PROPERTY AT 984 MASSACHUSETTS AVENUE FOR NEW FIREHOUSE... 4 ARTICLE 2 NEW FIREHOUSE DESIGN & BID FUNDING ... 9 ARTICLE 3 FIREHOUSE LAND AQUISITION: RELATED COSTS ... 144 2 TOWN OF BOXBOROUGH SPECIAL TOWN MEETING Monday, March 9, 2026 7:00 PM To either of the Constables of the Town of Boxborough, Greetings: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby required to notify all residents of the Town of Boxborough, who shall be qualified to vote in accordance with the provisions of MGL Chapter 51, Section 1, to meet at the Blanchard Memorial School, 493 Massachusetts Avenue, Boxborough, MA starting on Monday, March 9, 2026 at 7:00 PM, to act on Articles 1 through 3 of this Special Town Meeting Warrant. 3 Dennis Reip, Town Moderator called the Special Town Meeting to order at 7:03 pm. A total of 334 registered voters attended. Robert Stemple, Select Board member, led the pledge of allegiance. Moderator Reip introduced the Town Clerk, Town Counsel, Town Administrator Michael Johns and the Select Board: Chair, Kristin Hilberg, Clerk Bob Stemple, Priya Sundaram, Wes Fowlks, and Sam Anderson. The Finance Committee: Chair Antony Newton, Vice-Chair, John Connor, Maria Neyland, Joe Stulpin, Michelle Ryan, and John Greven. He pointed out the Fire Station Building Committee in the front row. Moderator Reip introduced Assistant Town Administrator Rajon Hudson and Administrative Assistant, Kelley Price, running the slides. He thanked BXB-TV of Littleton Community Television for running the live stream and recording, Mark Crory, LCTV's Executive Director, LCTV’s Video Program Coordinators Judy Reid and Nicolas Casaletto. He thanked the Blanchard Memorial School principal, Michael Votto and Dan Ralls and his custodial staff and Ed Kukkula and the DPW for set up. The Boxborough Conservation Trust is hosting a refreshment table in the back. He reminded the voters about the Special Town Election on March 17, 2026 that is related to Articles 1 and 2. Moderator Reip explained the process of Town Meeting. He explained that there would be a Yes and No microphone for this town meeting. Motion on Reconsideration: Kristin Hilberg, Select Board Chair, moved and it was seconded that once final action has been taken on an Article, and the next order of business has been taken up, or the session of the Special Town Meeting has been adjourned, the Article may not again be considered at that Special Town Meeting unless the Moderator determines in his discretion that reconsideration would be in the best interest of the voters. Discussion on the motion: none Action on the motion: carried by a majority as declared by the Moderator. ARTICLE 1 PURCHASE OF PROPERTY AT 984 MASSACHUSETTS AVENUE FOR NEW FIREHOUSE $2,400,000 Bonding (Two-thirds Vote Required) Sponsor: Fire Station Building Committee Mary Brolin, Chair of the Fire Station Building Committee, moved and it was seconded that the Town vote to appropriate the sum of two million, four hundred thousand dollars ($2,400,000), to purchase, for public safety purposes including but not limited to construction of a new firehouse and all other related fire and emergency medical services or emergency management purposes, three contiguous parcels of land identified as 984 Massachusetts Avenue, Boxborough, Massachusetts, shown as Parcel ID 14-005-000 (984 Massachusetts Avenue), Parcel ID 14-003-000 (996 Massachusetts Avenue), and Parcel ID 14- 004-000 (38 Sara’s Way), and containing approximately 4.205 acres, including the payment of land acquisition costs and all other costs incidental or related thereto; that to meet this appropriation the Treasurer with the approval of the Select Board is authorized to borrow $2,400,000 under Chapter 44 of the General Laws or any other enabling authority and to issue bonds and notes of the Town 4 therefor; and, further, to authorize the Select Board to acquire the above-referenced parcels and enter into all agreements and execute any and all documents as may be necessary to effect said acquisition; provided, however, that this vote shall not take effect until the Town votes to exempt from the limitation on total taxes imposed by G.L. c.59, §21C (Proposition 2½) amounts required to pay the principal of and interest on the borrowing authorized by this vote. Summary: This article seeks Town Meeting authorization to purchase the three contiguous property lots located at 984 Massachusetts Avenue as a site for a new firehouse. The parcel allows for effective emergency response coverage and response times. The appropriation of $2,400,000 would cover the cost of the property acquisition. This article funds only the purchase of the land. A separate future Town Meeting vote would be required to fund construction of the new firehouse. The Fire Station Building Committee recommends (7-0-0). After considerable evaluation and analysis of 19 sites for viability, the Fire Station Building Committee (FSBC) is bringing forward one site for Town Meeting to vote on. The FSBC has put significant time and effort into the site selection. Overall, we evaluated 19 properties for the project. After initial assessment, we assessed five properties in depth, including 984 Massachusetts Avenue, 72 Stow Road, 1300 Massachusetts Avenue, 700-832 Massachusetts Avenue, and 502 Massachusetts Avenue, on 14 criteria including total project costs, how well the site could meet the operational needs of the fire department, the impact to abutters, and sustainability. Based on these criteria and all the data provided to us, we felt strongly that 984 Massachusetts Avenue offers the best overall solution for the Town. The 984 Massachusetts Avenue property is conveniently located on Massachusetts Avenue, is not in a residential neighborhood, has flexibility to fit the program, and is located well to serve the needs of the more densely populated areas of Town. Based on all these factors, the Fire Station Building Committee recommends this purchase. Presentation by the FSBC was given by Chair, Mary Brolin. She summarized the benefits of the site and how the site came to be available. The presentation included information about why a new firehouse is needed, the roadmap forward, and the tax impact. The timeline of the history of the firehouse was explained, starting 64 years ago. The safety, security, and non-compliance with NFPA, Building and Fire and OSHA codes were explained. She explained that the owner of 984 Mass Ave approached the Fire Chief about selling his property for the Fire House after the vote at Fall Town Meeting that allowed for zoning for this purpose. This offer was discussed with the Town Administrator and the FSBC, and a letter of intent to purchase has been signed. This agreement is good until early April, and the FSBC believes that this is a good opportunity, pending approval at Town Meeting and Special Town Election for borrowing. Ms. Brolin spoke about how the town has changed since the Fire House was built, completed in 1962. She talked about the various changes in needs and services over the past 6 decades, and how the building has not changed to keep up with those, with current hazardous and unsafe conditions for the staff. Various committees have spent almost 15 years on this initial phase of attempting to build a new Fire House. The current committee, convened in 2024, has conducted over 20 forums and public meetings. Over 20 properties have been investigated. In the fall, new sites were raised as possibilities. There were multiple rounds of assessments on several sites; in January 2026 984 Mass Ave was unanimously selected by the FSBC and supported by Finance Committee and Select Board. This site 5 avoids abutter concerns and minimizes costly legal delays and traffic concerns. She showed a map of the site and a conceptual layout of the building on the site. She described the tax impact of Article 1: starting in 2027, the tax impact would be about $76 on a $1 million house. She went on to describe the estimated construction costs at $32 million, which will be bonded over 30 years; the intent is to come back to Town Meeting next year with the actual bid in hand, with an aim to reduce the total costs during the design phase. The design and purchase costs will be wrapped into this bond. The estimate is $1,092 per year on a home value of $1 million. Because building costs escalate at least 4-5% each year, delays will cost us more. The Finance Committee recommends (6-0-0). Maria Neyland gave the Finance Committee recommendation. The Fin Com unanimously recommends this article. After years of studying multiple locations, and many opportunities for the public to comment, the Fire Station Building Committee (FSBC) has recommended 984 Massachusetts Avenue for the site of the a much-needed new fire station. The Finance Committee supports purchasing 984 Massachusetts Avenue for the new fire station. The site’s design flexibility and the early positive engagement with the abutters minimizes the risk of costly legal and construction delays. Furthermore, securing this location helps to ensure the safety and retention of firefighters by beginning to address the hazardous living /work conditions at the current station. This site deceases the risk of further project delays that would otherwise force the Town to incur the significant additional expense of providing temporary housing for our firefighting staff. For these reasons, the Finance Committee supports purchasing the 984 Massachusetts Avenue site to build a new fire station. Funding for this article will be through a short-term Bond Anticipation Note (BAN). The BAN will be refinanced into a long-term construction bond, coming for a vote in 2027. Estimated Cost to Taxpayer Land Purchase – 30 Year Bond Bond amount Annual Debt Service (Principal and Interest) Tax per $1,000 Tax per average house Assumption: Average house value Assumption: Town Value Estimated Amount $2,400,000 $148,800 $0.08 $76 $980,490 $1,915,013,882 The Select Board recommends (5-0-0). The Select Board unanimously recommends this article. Priya Sundaram gave the Select Board recommendation. The Select Board notes that Boxborough’s search for a suitable ﬁre sta on site has been ongoing for more than ﬁ een years and has involved mul ple boards and commitees. A primary challenge throughout this process has been iden fying a loca on that is centrally situated, not in a neighborhood, large enough to accommodate a modern ﬁre sta on that meets current codes and opera onal standards, and available at a reasonable cost to the Town. 6 The property at 984 Massachusets Avenue meets all of these criteria. The site is located on Massachusets Avenue with clear access and sight lines, is not situated in a neighborhood as compared to other loca ons such as Stow Road, and provides more than four acres of land, suﬃcient to support the required ﬁre sta on program. The proposed purchase price of approximately $2.4 million represents a reasonable and responsible cost for a site of this size and loca on. In addi on, this site is closer to the Town’s more densely populated areas and oﬀers improved emergency response coverage when compared to the exis ng ﬁre sta on. For these reasons, the Select Board supports the acquisi on of this property and recommends approval of this ar cle. 7 Discussion on Article 1: John Fallon of Paddock Ln thanked the many building committee members over the years for their work on this project. He emphasized the dire need for a new fire station and talked about how this site fits all of the criteria. Thomas Horsky of Depot Rd asked what the cost would be of renovating the current fire station. Mary Brolin said that the previous building committee looked into this and found that it was not feasible to renovate and it would need to be a rebuild, with an increased cost. There are severe limitations with the current site and it would have been more expensive to house the firefighters and the site has major limitations that make it challenging to meet the code and needs of the fire station. It would have been a less than optimal build for more money. Kathy Luce of Emanuel Dr said she’s fully in support of this article and spoke about how long this has been under discussion (her kids were in preschool when first starting to talk about this need and now they are in college and grad school). She asked what the next step would be if this article is not approved. Mary Brolin said that they need a new fire station and the agreement with the owner is through early April. She is not sure if he would be willing to wait; if not, the station would go to the next site under consideration which would likely be 72 Stow Rd. Having no new fire station is really not an option. Robert Hendrie of Cobleigh Rd said we are spending a lot of money in a bad economic time. He disagrees with the economics. He asked what would happen to the current fire station. Kristin Hilberg stated that that would be the purview of the select board and there are many ideas floated such as a community center, etc., and will be looking for public input when the time comes. Andrew Gruskay of Daniel’s Way asked what the Fire Chief’s opinion is of this new fire station. Chief Kivlan said they are very excited about this new site and this opportunity. Andrew Gruskay asked if there have been firefighters that have left because of the conditions. Chief Kivlan has lost about 4 firefighters in the past year and a half that have left and have said in their exit interviews that the conditions were a factor in their departure, even if not the main reason. David Rocheleau of Liberty Square Rd said that an acre of land is worth about $250-300k/acre so why would we be spending over $500k/acre? Kristin Hilberg spoke about the market value of the land and explained that the land was bought for $2.25 million in 2023 and then the lot was improved. The last lot she closed on was $450k for a single house lot. The cost is $2.4 million not $4 million. David Rocheleau asked where the property is and there was further discussion about the location. He disputed that there were more people living on the west side of town. Chief Kivlan explained that there is more density of housing units on the west side of town. Mr. Rocheleau said that brick and mortar condos would not burn, whereas houses are made of wood. Chief Kivlan reminded the speaker about the major fire on Swanson Rd at the condos several years ago. Mark Barbadoro of Old Harvard Rd commented that 20% of the town lives on the other side of 495 and that there was a disastrous fire in the condos on Swanson Rd about 5 years ago that displaced at least 8 25 families. He commended the FSBC for their plasticity in moving to this site, away from the previous site that they had chosen. He pointed out that it is mostly on lithic bedrock and that this would cause problems potentially for drainage and septic systems. He wondered if the costs of complicated septic and stormwater management systems have been accounted for in this cost. He stated that he is voting for the article regardless. Mary Brolin asked if Steve Kirby, the Owners Project Manager from Vertex could speak and Dennis Reip allowed it. Steve Kirby, the OPM, spoke about the costs included in the design budget including a possible raised septic with a pump. There is contingency money in the design costs and increased $ to address some of the complexities. There have been test pits and our resident hydrologist, Grant Garven has found that there is favorable bedrock for drilling of wells. Andew Tavolacci of Old Harvard Rd asked if Article 1 and 2 are linked. Article 2 is not contingent on a specific site? Mary Brolin said they are technically not linked. We could still vote Article 2 even if Article 1 doesn’t pass. Andrew Tavolacci asked about the need for a traffic light at 984 Mass Ave. Mary Brolin said that a traffic study was done and would not need a light, but we may do another traffic study under design just to be sure, and clarified that it would be paid for by us, working with the state. Kate Davies of Guggins Ln asked why we have to buy the land before the design is done. She is very much in support of this Article. Mary Brolin said that the design needs to be specific to the site and we need to get on the site to do all of the testing and the owner has let us on for preliminary testing but it isn’t clear if he would allow us on for further testing. There are a lot of specifics about site that will drive design and costs. Mary Nadwairski of Stonehedge Place moved the question and it was seconded. Action on the motion to stop debate: carried by 2/3s as declared by the Moderator. Action on the motion on Article 1: carried by 2/3s as declared by the Moderator. ARTICLE 2 NEW FIREHOUSE DESIGN & BID FUNDING $2,765,910 Bonding (Two-thirds Vote Required) Sponsor: Fire Station Building Committee Mary Brolin, Chair of the Fire Station Building Committee, moved and it was seconded that the Town vote to appropriate the sum of two million, seven hundred sixty-five thousand, nine hundred ten dollars ($2,765,910), to design, prepare construction drawings, pre-qualify contractors, bid the construction, and determine the lowest responsible general bid for a new firehouse, including the payment of costs incidental or related thereto; that to meet this appropriation the Treasurer with the approval of the Select Board is authorized to borrow $2,765,910 under Chapter 44 of the General Laws or any other enabling authority and to issue bonds and notes of the Town therefor; provided, however, that this vote shall not take effect until the Town votes to exempt from the limitation on total taxes imposed by G.L. c.59, §21C (Proposition 2½) amounts required to pay the principal of and interest on the borrowing authorized by this vote. 9 Summary: Over the past 20 months, the Fire Station Building Committee (FSBC) has worked closely with Vertex, our Owner’s Project Manager (OPM), and Context Architecture to review parcels of land for their feasibility to situate a new firehouse and develop the cost estimate for this article. Voting yes for this article will provide funding for the Town’s OPM, architect, and consultant team to move from conceptual design to complete design and bidding. This phase will include construction drawings with a mitigation plan, prequalification of bidders, bidding of the project, and selection of the lowest qualified general bidder. We will then come back to the voters at a future town meeting with the full, exact price to construct and deliver a new firehouse, including all furniture, fixtures, landscape, and demolition of building(s) on site. For the design and bid work, the cost is $2,765,910. The Fire Station Building Committee recommends (7-0-0). Mary Brolin gave the recommendation and presentation. After considerable evaluation and analysis of 19 sites and plans for the new firehouse, the FSBC has recommended a location for the new firehouse. The next critical step is to design the firehouse and get bids for the new firehouse so we know the actual costs. At this time, we have a conceptual estimate, but the design phase involves three interactive phases of designing the building, getting cost estimates, and value engineering to keep the building at the lowest cost possible while meeting the functional needs. May 19, 2026 4 CONSENT AGENDA INFORMATION In an effort to streamline Annual Town Meeting and make it more accessible and efficient for voters, the Select Board will again use Consent Agendas. This process helps expedite the passage of articles that the Select Board, after consulting with Town Counsel, the Moderator, and the Finance Committee, believes are not expected to generate controversy and may appropriately be acted upon without debate. The purpose of a Consent Agenda is to allow motions under designated articles to be considered together as one unit and voted on without debate. This year, there will be 5 Consent Agendas: 1. Non-Financial Consent Agenda (Articles 13 through 14)1 Includes routine administrative and procedural articles that do not involve financial appropriations and are not expected to require discussion. 2. Financial (Non-Capital) Consent Agenda (Articles 15 through 24) 2 Includes non-capital financial articles such as standard financial and administrative items, operational and maintenance expenses, employee-related costs, public safety needs, and other standard financial and compliance items. 3. Capital Consent Agenda (Articles 26 through 41) 3 Includes capital purchases and projects such as equipment, technology, facility improvements, and public safety investments that support ongoing Town operations and infrastructure. 4. Two-Thirds Vote Articles (Articles 42 through 43) 4 Includes articles that require a two-thirds vote under Massachusetts General Law. While grouped for efficiency, each article within this Consent Agenda will still require a two-thirds vote for passage. 5. Community Preservation Committee (CPC) Consent Agenda (Articles 44 through 50) 5 Includes Community Preservation Act projects related to open space, historic preservation, community housing, and recreation, as recommended through the Community Preservation Committee process. At the call of each Consent Agenda, the Moderator will announce the number of each article. If one or more voters object to including any particular article in the Consent Agenda, they should say the word “Hold” in a loud voice when the number is called. That article will then be removed from the Consent Agenda and restored to its original place in the Warrant, where it will be debated and voted on in the usual manner. After all articles in the Consent Agenda have been called, the Moderator will ask that all remaining articles be voted as a unit. Voters are encouraged to carefully review the list of articles proposed for each Consent Agenda. Summaries are included under each article as printed in this Warrant. 2026 Annual Town Meeting (FY27) Warrant - May 19, 2026 5 May 19, 2026 Tellers were sworn in: Kim Grotbek, Cassie LaRussa, John Fallon, Tim Rudolph, Leah Wofsy and Justin Rowe. A total of 161 registered voters checked in (3.9% of 4,087 registered voters). There was only one night of Town Meeting this year. He introduced the Finance Committee Chair, Antony Newton, and the members introduced themselves: John Connor, Vice Chair and Clerk, John Greven, Maria Neyland, and Joseph Stulpin. Michelle Ryan was absent. Administrative Assistant, Kelley Price, and Town Planner, Alec Wade were introduced, running the projector, showing the motions and presentations on the screen. He introduced the town Finance Director Honghoa Le to assist with any financial facts of the matter. He recognized that Rajon Hudson, Assistant Town Administrator is not present due to being with his family as his mother receives end of life care. In the front row of chairs are members of the School Committee and Planning Board There are numerous town department heads and staff, our chiefs of police and fire, as well as members of volunteer boards and committees on hand to speak to some of the motions as needed. This meeting is being broadcast live and is also being recorded for on demand viewing on BXB-TV by Littleton Community Television (LCTV). Mr. Reip expressed his thanks to LCTV's Executive Director Mark Crory, LCTV’s Video Program Coordinator Judy Reid and Nick Casteletto and the rest of their crew. On behalf of the Town, Mr. Reip extended thanks to the Blanchard School’s principal Michael Votto for being a gracious host and Blanchard School’s Dan Ralls and his staff and to Ed Kukkula and our DPW staff for preparing the gym for tonight’s Town Meeting. 2026 Annual Town Meeting (FY27) Warrant - May 19, 2026 6 Announcements Non-voters over the age of 18 need to sit in the BACK of the hall in the area marked off to the side on the right as you are facing the stage. Refreshments at the back of the hall are being provided by the Boxborough Conservation Trust. Town Meeting will be tonight, and if voters approve the proposed procedural motion a bit later on, will continue, if needed, to tomorrow Wednesday May 20th and Thursday May 21st if needed. Boxborough’s Municipal Election is TUESDAY, June 2nd, 7:00 am to 8:00 pm at Town Hall. There are contested races for seats on the Select Board, Planning Board, and School Committee along with unopposed candidates seeking re-election to the Board of Health, Library Trustees, and Town Moderator positions. Please consider the candidates and VOTE next week. He went on to explain Town Meeting process. The agenda for this meeting is the Warrant. Everything we discuss at this meeting is contained in the warrant. This is not a public hearing or forum for random matters of interest and we will not be discussing anything that is not already identified in the Warrant. The Warrant includes summaries and recommendations for each article. In addition to the Warrant, material on the tables in the back of room includes a postcard with a QR code to the detailed FY26 school budget book, the 2025 Town Report, a Resident Survey QR code, and a Guide to Town Meeting. Mr. Reip explained that his job as Moderator is to be the presiding officer of this legislature. The Boxborough Town Meeting process is guided by Town Meeting Time, a handbook of parliamentary law prepared by the Massachusetts Moderators Association. He is here to ensure that Town Meeting is: Fair: There is a set of rules and everyone follows them Open: Everyone who wishes to speak has the opportunity to do so Civil: Everyone listens respectfully. One part of being civil is that there is no applause or booing during discussion of articles. Relevant: All the discussion, motions, and amendments must be “within the four corners” of the motion on the floor, and voters must be notified in advance of the items to be discussed at Town Meeting by way of the Warrant. We vote on MOTIONS which might be slightly different from the wording of the Articles printed in the warrant. The motions will be displayed on the screen. Starting on page 8 of the Warrant you will find the Town Meeting Guide which summarizes the process with some of the most common motions listed. Voters were given a 1-page handout on “Boxborough Town Meeting Process” as they walked in. Four key points: a) To be recognized to speak you need to be at one of the two microphones. 2026 Annual Town Meeting (FY27) Warrant - May 19, 2026 7 b) Speakers must state their name and address for the record and are limited to 3 minutes. There will be a clock for all to see here up on the screen. c) All discussion must be relevant to the Motions on the floor d) Mr. Reip will call for a vote when no one is standing at microphone. If someone wants to end debate before that they need to come to a microphone and say “I move the question” and we will vote on stopping debate. Sponsors of the article cannot move the question. Voters cannot make comments at the mic, and then immediately move the question. Mr. Reip may call for votes to be made simply by voice, yea or nay, or a show of hands using the green cards, or if necessary, by a standing count. All voters should have received a “bright green” card when you signed in. For anything other than a voice vote, you need to have a green card to vote and for your vote to be counted. When he asks for a vote by a show of hands, he will ask you to raise the card to make it easier for to see. If we go to a standing count, he’ll ask you to show your card to be counted. Under town bylaw Mr. Reip has the ability to declare a majority or a 2/3 vote using the voice vote or show of hands vote methods. If he does so, and seven voters think he was in error, please say so immediately and we will have a standing counted vote instead. Note: if anyone has a question about process you can stand in place at any time and say “Point of Order” in a loud voice and direct your question to the Moderator. Except for a point of order, you MUST be at a microphone to ask a question, make a comment, or make a motion to move the question. We will have two microphones tonight and I will be recognizing people to speak in an alternating fashion. I will refer to these as the microphone to my right (your left), and the microphone to my left (your right). Please note the chairs along the aisles directly behind each microphone that are intended for people waiting in line at the microphones. Please leave these seats open for folks lining up to speak. Please remember to keep the discussion CIVIL and disagree without being disagreeable. Boxborough has a long tradition of civility at TM. Let’s continue this tradition here tonight. Acton-Boxborough School Committee delivered a report. Vice Chair, Adam Klein gave the school district report and budget. He thanked retiring committee members. He stated that he would be taking a different approach from past reports, highlighting this pivotal moment, rather than the past year’s accomplishments. Our enrollment has dropped by 600 students and because we are a wealthy town we don’t get a lot of state aid. He spoke about how the budget is put together. There have been double-digit increases in health insurance, retirement, state-mandated tuition, and other costs. Cuts were made in 2022 through 2024. They reduced spending and classroom assistants, and finally teaching positions and basic supplies. The previous year’s Elementary Budget Task Force reduced classroom assistants and shared specialized staff across schools. The class sizes are pushing the limits of the school committee guidelines. There was a $3 million gap. The financial situation made it necessary to rethink how the schools are organized, and the strategic planning process of AB Forward is a five-year process that was begun this year. The committee engaged the community throughout the process. More than 6,000 survey responses have been received, over 1,000 emails received, and over 20 hours of public comments and questions. The plan is to consolidate schools, avoiding $40-80 million in future costs, and saves nearly $17 million over ten years. text: Select Board Chair Statement - FY27 Budget Good evening, Iwant to take a moment to speak not just about the numbers in front of you, butabouUvbat they mean to all of us who live here in Cotain This year's budget is, in many ways, a holding-the-line budget. On the municipal side, we have worked very hard to keep spending essentially flat. Departments have come forward with thoughtful requests, and inmany cases, those requests have beenreduced or deferred in order to make this budget work. But Iwant to be very clear, just because the town budget is not increasing does not mean costs are not rising. They are. We are seeing continued increases in school assessments, in regional obligations, in benefits, and in the everyday costs of running a town. Those pressures are real, and they affect all of us, especially our residents who are already struggling to afford to stay here. We are increasingly hearing from people—long-time residents, seniors, families—who are worried about whether they can continue to afford Colrain. At the same time, we are being asked to support significant capital investments at the school level, and to respond to growing needs in our community. We have an aging population. We know that. And we also know that we do not yet have the level of services and facilities that our seniors deserve. Ido not want to see services like our library or our Council on Aging fall behind or be diminished. Ifanything, we should be thtnlring about how to strengthen them over time. So we are trying to balance all of this by: • Keepingthe budget as stable as possible, increasing fees to users and utilizing gifts and grants. We shouldn't be afraid to ask people to pay for or donate to services they • receive the benefit of Continuing to support essential services while recognizing the real financial pressure on taxpayers • And planning for a fixture that includes both our schools and our aging community. This is not easy. There are no simple solutions. What you see in this budget reflects difficult trade-offs and a deep commitment the Boardhas to our community, all of which are shared with our amazing staff and department heads. We are not expanding services this year. We are maintaining and trying to improve efficiency. Tonight I ask that you support this budget as a responsible and necessary step in keeping Colrain operations stable as we continue to work cooperatively with our school partners and our neighbors in the region. But, please understand, as we move forward, these challenges are not going away. Decisions that impact the next generations of our town are directly in front of us. That is why conversations about long-termplanning, growth, and community investment are so important. Thank you for supporting me as I've grown inthis position. Please consider serving on one of our boards or committees. There has never been a more important time for our community to lock arms to move toward a sustainable future. O 2Districts8Towns SUSTAINABILITY STUDY: ONE PAGE OVERVIEW Spring 2026 B What is the Sustainability Study? The 2 district 8 towns Sustainability Committee was organized to study and analyze the operating and organizational structures of the Mohawk Trail and Hawlemont school districts in light of ongoing enrollment, fiscal and educational pressures. Formed in early 2024, the Committee's goal is to develop a plan to provide students with a broad array of high-quality educational opportunities that prepare them for future success - in college, career and life - and to do so in a sustainable way that our rural towns can afford. This document provides stakeholders with a concise, factual summary of the 2D8T Sustainability Study, the Steering Committee's recommended Plan of Action, and the ongoing work being done to provide additional detail to the Plan and address questions raised by stakeholders. We encourage informed dialogue and constructive feedback as this process continues. (sf Why Conduct the Study Q*. How the Study Was Conducted Mohawk Trail and Hawlemont face critical challenges that affect most rural districts: declining enrollment, rising costs, flat state aid, and increasing student needs. Without action, these challenges will continue to produce budget deficits, cuts to educational programming and staff, rising town assessments, and limited academic and social opportunities for students. Over 16+ months, the Steering Committee, composed of community members and district leadership, supported and reviewed in-depth analysis of current educational programming, enrollment, staffing, finance, facilities, and transportation. Initial findings were shared in extensive outreach communities and staff, and the input received has helped shape the ongoing work. im Models Examined After reviewing 177 ideas offered by stakeholders and staff, 5 operational models were selected for detailed review: 1. Status Quo 4. Partial Elementary Consolidation No change to existing operations Consolidate elementary students into fewer schools 2. Merger 5. Create a Single PreK-12 Campus Consolidate all elementary schools and create a single PreK-12 on the Mohawk Trail site Merger of Mohawk Trail and Hawlemont 3. Move Grade 6 Create a Grade 6-3 middle school on the Mohawk Trail campus t Key Findings of Comprehensive Option Analysis • • • Maintaining the Status Quo does not address existing fiscal or educational challenges. A single campus provides the greatest opportunity for long-term fiscal Sustainability. Larger student bodies best support robust academic and social environments; ensure equitable access to academics, student supports, co- and extra-curricular activities; and encourage strong professional collaboration. • Creating a single campus will require some modifications to existing Mohawk Trail facilities. SUSTAINABILITY STUDY OVERVIEW (CONTINUED) Steering Committee Recommendation In Spring 2025, The Steering Committee and both School Committees voted to pursue the aspirational goal of educating all students at a single PK-12 campus at Mohawk Trail. - and to complete additional work to better understand potential outcomes, address community concerns and develop detailed operational and educational plans. This goal would be achieved gradually over 5-7 years. No specific decisions have been made. Educational visioning work (now underway) will determine specific needs. Goal: To the extent possible, manage reductions through retirement and staff turnover. Recommended by Finance Committee. Explanation: This continues to fund the Town’s liability for post-employment benefits for Town employees. ___ ARTICLE 13. To see if the Town will vote to transfer from Free Cash to the General Stabilization Fund the sum of $185,000, or take any action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to transfer the sum of One Hundred Eighty-Five Thousand Dollars ($185,000) from Free Cash to the Town’s General Stabilization Fund. Recommended by Finance Committee. Explanation: Adding funds to the General Stabilization Fund helps maintain the Town’s financial health and assists in generating interest revenue. ___ 4 MOTIONS ARTICLE 14. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from the Highway Vehicle Stabilization Fund, or borrow a sum of money for the purchase of a new Highway Department grader, said funds to be used in addition to any funds granted by the Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT) through its Grant Central program, and to authorize the Select Board to enter into all agreements and take all necessary actions to accept and expend such grant funds, provided that a local match is authorized by this vote, or take any action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to approve the purchase of a new Highway Department grader for the sum of Four Hundred and Sixty Thousand Dollars ($460,000), and to fund said purchase by transferring the sum of Two Hundred and Ten Thousand Dollars ($210,000) from the Highway Vehicle Stabilization Fund and expending Two Hundred and Fifty Thousand Dollars ($250,000) from a Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT) grant through its Grant Central program, and to authorize the Select Board to enter into all agreements and take all necessary actions to accept and expend such funds and to purchase such grader. Recommended by Finance Committee. Explanation: This will allow the Town to purchase a new Highway Department grader if the Town receives the grant award and allows for the required match. ___ ARTICLE 15. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from the Highway Vehicle Stabilization Fund the sum of $85,000 for the rehabilitation and restoration of 2001 International Chassis for use as a highway vehicle, or take any action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to transfer the sum of Eighty-Five Thousand Dollars ($85,000) from the Highway Vehicle Stabilization Fund for the rehabilitation and restoration of the 2001 International Chassis for use as a highway vehicle. Recommended by Finance Committee. Explanation: This will allow the Highway Department to build a large truck to use for snow removal operations using the Fire Department surplus vehicle chassis. ___ ARTICLE 16. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from Free Cash the sum of $10,000 for the purchase of an Everest CK 640 Snowplow to be used by the Highway Department, or take any other action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to transfer the sum of Ten Thousand Dollars ($10,000) from Free Cash for the purchase of an Everest CK 640 Snowplow to be used by the Highway Department. Explanation: This will fund the purchase of a new snowplow requested by the Highway Department. ___ ARTICLE 17. To see if the Town will vote to create a special purpose stabilization fund pursuant to G.L. c.40, §5B for the design, construction, reconstruction, and major repair of Townowned buildings and facilities; or take any action relative thereto. 2/3 Vote Required. 5 MOTIONS MOTION: Move the Town vote to create a Facilities Stabilization Fund, which shall be a special purpose stabilization fund pursuant to G.L. c.40, §5B for the purpose of funding design, construction, reconstruction, and capital repairs of Town-owned buildings and facilities. Recommended by Finance Committee. Explanation: This will allow the Town to create a Facilities Stabilization Fund for the designated purpose identified. ___ ARTICLE 18. To see if the Town will vote to operate the Broadband Enterprise Fund by raising and appropriating or transferring from available funds, the total sum of $744,618, or take any other action related thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to appropriate the following sums to operate the Broadband Enterprise Fund: Cost Salaries/Wages Expenses Debt Service Indirect Costs Total: Amount $ 8,000 $557,093 $162,625 $ 16,900 $744,618 and to raise said sums from the following: Source Enterprise Receipts Total: Amount $744,618 $744,618 Recommended by Finance Committee. Explanation: Funding supports the operation and maintenance of the Town’s broadband services and allows for the Town to cover the overhead of services provided. ___ ARTICLE 19. To see if the Town will vote Town to approve annual spending limits for Revolving Funds established in the Town Bylaws, pursuant to .G.L. c.44, §53E½, for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026, or take any action relative thereto. Authorized Revolving Funds Plumbing Inspections Electrical Inspections Fire Inspections Building Department Dog Fund Department, Board/Committee Agency or Officer Plumbing Inspector Electrical Inspector Fire Chief Building Commissioner Town Clerk 6 Fiscal Year Expenditure Limit $3,500 $3,500 $3,500 $15,000 $15,000 MOTIONS MOTION: Move the Town vote to approve annual spending limits as listed below for Revolving Funds established in the Town Bylaws, pursuant to G.L. c.44, §53E½, for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026. Recommended by Finance Committee. Authorized Revolving Funds Plumbing Inspections Electrical Inspections Fire Inspections Building Department Dog Fund Department, Board/Committee Agency or Officer Plumbing Inspector Electrical Inspector Fire Chief Building Commissioner Town Clerk Fiscal Year Expenditure Limit $3,500 $3,500 $3,500 $15,000 $15,000 Explanation: This article sets spending limits to ensure the responsible use of already-authorized revolving funds. ___ ARTICLE 20. To see if the town will vote to authorize the Select Board to apply for, accept, and expend state or federal grants that may become available, or take any action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to authorize the Select Board to apply for, accept, and expend any state or federal grants that may become available. Explanation: This article allows the Town to seek and utilize grant funding sources for various projects and initiatives. ___ ARTICLE 21. To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Select Board to enter into contracts with the Massachusetts Department of Transportation for construction and/or maintenance of highways or other permissible expenditures from the Transportation Bond monies (Chapter 90) and authorize the Select Board to accept any monies from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for highway construction and/or maintenance related work, or take any action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to authorize the Select Board to enter into contracts with the Massachusetts Department of Transportation for the construction and/or maintenance of highways, whether pursuant to G.L. c.90 or any other enabling authority, and to accept any monies from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for highway construction and/or maintenance related work. Explanation: This article facilitates the Town’s ability to manage and fund highway construction and maintenance projects. ___ ARTICLE 22. To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Treasurer to borrow in anticipation of Chapter 90 State reimbursement funds for road repair projects, or take any action relative thereto. 7 MOTIONS MOTION: Move the Town vote to authorize the Treasurer to borrow in anticipation of Chapter 90 state reimbursement funds for road repair projects. Explanation: This article ensures the Town can finance road repair projects while awaiting state reimbursement. ___ ARTICLE 23. To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Treasurer to enter into compensating balance agreements during Fiscal Year 2027 as permitted by Massachusetts G.L. c.44, §53F, or take any action relative thereto. MOTION: Move the Town vote to authorize the Treasurer to enter into compensating balance agreements during Fiscal Year 2027 pursuant to G.L. c.44, §53F. Explanation: This article allows the Town to manage its funds efficiently through compensating balance agreements. A compensating balance is a minimum balance that an organization agrees to maintain in its bank account as part of receiving favorable loans or other services from a bank. ___ ARTICLE 24. To see if the Town will vote to amend the Town of Colrain Zoning Bylaws to substitute the term “Select Board” for the term “Board of Selectmen”; to substitute the word “Selectpersons” for the word “Selectmen”; and to substitute the word “Selectperson” for the word “Selectman”; and further affirm that upon the effective date of such amendment, the term “Board of Selectmen” shall be taken to mean “Select Board” and the term “Selectmen” shall be taken to mean “Selectpersons” and the term “Selectman” shall be taken to mean “Selectperson” for the purposes of all laws, regulations, contracts, agreements, or other documents that refer to or are applicable to the Town of Colrain Zoning Bylaws, or take any action relative thereto. 2/3 Vote Required. MOTION: Move the Town vote to amend the Town of Colrain Zoning Bylaws to substitute the term “Select Board” for the term “Board of Selectmen”; to substitute the word “Selectpersons” for the word “Selectmen”; and to substitute the word “Selectperson” for the word “Selectman”; and further affirm that upon the effective date of such amendment, the term “Board of Selectmen” shall be taken to mean “Select Board” and the term “Selectmen” shall be taken to mean “Selectpersons” and the term “Selectman” shall be taken to mean “Selectperson” for the purposes of all laws, regulations, contracts, agreements, or other documents that refer to or are applicable to the Town of Colrain Zoning Bylaws. ___ ARTICLE 25. To see if the Town will vote to approve the warrant article, “Resolution in Support of an ‘Act Establishing Medicare for All’”, or take any action relative thereto. text: TOWN OF DOVER ___ WARRANT for the ANNUAL TOWN MEETING Monday, May 4, 2026 and Monday, May 11, 2026 (should Town Meeting need to continue to a second evening) 7:00 PM Dover-Sherborn Regional High School Mudge Auditorium and TOWN ELECTIONS Monday, May 18, 2026 7:00 AM – 8:00 PM Dover Town House ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 To the Residents of Dover: This Warrant provides notification of the 2026 Annual Town Meeting and Town Election. It advises residents of the various issues being considered at the business meeting scheduled for May 4th and the Offices on the ballot for the Town Election on May 18th. Only Articles listed in this Warrant may come before residents for a vote. Articles for the Annual Town Meeting are grouped in four categories: Financial and Budget; Zoning, Planning, and Land Use; General Articles, and the Tax Rate. The most important votes that take place at the Annual Town Meeting are related to the budget. We urge citizens to read the budget, understand it, and help us foster excellence within the community. The Town website, https://www.doverma.gov/453/Town-Meeting, includes the most recent version of the FY2027 Budget and other financial Articles as well as other relevant information for each Article. A comprehensive budget recommendation for FY2027 will be delivered to all households in mid-April in the Warrant Committee Report and Recommendations for the Annual Town Meeting, also referred to as the ‘Blue Book’ (for its color). The Blue Book will provide much more detail and explanation of each Article. We recommend you bring a copy of the Blue Book to Town Meeting. About Town Meeting: Sometimes referred to as the oldest form of government in the country, Town Meeting is your opportunity to learn about, participate, and vote in Dover’s Town Government. Please consider spending a few hours of your time to attend this year’s Town Meeting and play a role in the direction of your Town. Thank you. Dover Board of Selectmen Robyn Hunter, Chair David M. Haviland, Clerk Cam Hudson, Member 2 ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 Norfolk, ss. To any of the Constables of the Town of Dover in said County, Greetings; In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts you are hereby required to notify and warn the inhabitants of the Town of Dover, qualified as the Constitution requires to vote in elections and in Town affairs, to meet in the Mudge Auditorium at the Dover-Sherborn Regional High School in said Town on Monday, the 4th day of May, 2026, at seven o'clock in the evening then and there to act on the following articles, to wit: Article 1. Hear/Act on Committee Reports (Board of Selectmen) To hear and act on the various reports of the various committees: (a) (b) As contained in the printed 2025 Annual Report; and Any other reports submitted to the voters by the Town Committees. FINANCE/BUDGET ARTICLES Article 2. Establish Salaries for Elected Officials for FY2027 (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will set the salaries for its elected officials for the ensuing fiscal year; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 3. Authorize Amounts for Revolving Funds (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote pursuant to Section 5-16 (Finances) of the General Bylaws of the Town of Dover to authorize the use of revolving fund accounts for the following boards or departments, and that unless otherwise amended by the Board of Selectmen and Warrant Committee, such accounts shall not exceed the following amounts for Fiscal Year 2027: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Building Department Gas, Plumbing, and Wiring Inspectors $68,900 Board of Health Inspections and permitting; Operation of immunizations and other health programs $25,000 Library Materials replacement $ 5,000 Council on Aging Senior activities and transportation $40,000 Recycling Committee Purchase of materials for sale $ 4,000 3 ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 6. 7. 8. 9. Department of Public Works Maintenance, repair, and replacement of facilities and equipment for the Transfer Station $35,000 Community Center Costs associated with operating the Community Center and maintenance/improvement projects for the facility $25,000 Cemetery Commission Cost for weekend and after hour burials; Columbarium related expenses $30,000 Stormwater Tree Mitigation Town stormwater mitigation improvements, including planting and maintenance of trees, and stormwater regulatory compliance $30,000; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 4. Appropriate the FY2027 Operating Budget (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for salaries and expenditures by departments, officers, boards, and committees of the Town for the ensuing fiscal year; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 5. Appropriate the FY2027 Capital Budget (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, borrow or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for the various capital purposes listed below; and to determine if any amount borrowed under this article shall be contingent upon the passage of a ballot question exempting the amounts required to pay for the bonds from the provisions of Proposition 2 ½; or take any other action relative thereto: 1. Fire Department/Ambulance (a) Breathing Air Compressor/Fill Station 2. Police Department (a) Patrol Vehicles (b) Tasers and Accessories 3. Police/Fire (a) Public Safety Building Feasibility Study 4 ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 4. Department of Public Works (a) Town Fuel Island Replacement (b) Dump Truck with Plow and Spreader (c) Backhoe with Plow (d) Mower (e) Radio Upgrades (f) Town Center (Springdale/Walpole/Centre) Intersection Improvements (g) Caryl Park Water System Repair 5. Selectmen (a) Town House Boiler Repair (b) Town House HVAC Feasibility Study 6. Parks and Recreation (a) Caryl Park Parking Lot Improvements and New Pickleball Courts Article 6. Appropriate for Dover-Sherborn Regional Schools Capital Expenses To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, borrow, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for the purpose of paying the costs of various items of capital equipment and improvements, pursuant to an intergovernmental agreement with the Dover-Sherborn Regional School District and the Town of Sherborn; and to determine if any amount borrowed under this article shall be contingent upon the passage of a ballot question exempting the amounts required to pay for the bonds from the provisions of Proposition 2 ½; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 7. Appropriate for Unemployment Compensation Fund (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for the purpose of funding an unemployment compensation fund as authorized by Chapter 40, Section 5E, of the Massachusetts General Laws; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 8. Appropriate for Sick Leave for Retiring Police Officers (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money to provide for the payment of accumulated sick leave to retired police officers as authorized by Chapter 375 of the Acts of 1984; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 9. Appropriate for Road Construction, Reconstruction and Improvements (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, borrow or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for the purpose of highway construction, reconstruction and other improvements under the authority of the Massachusetts General Laws as funded by various State budgets; and to authorize the Selectmen to enter into contracts, apply for, 5 ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 accept, expend, and borrow in anticipation of State aid for such projects; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 10. Appropriate to Conservation Fund (Conservation Commission) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for the Conservation Fund to be used by the Conservation Commission for any purpose authorized by Chapter 40, Section 8C of the Massachusetts General Laws; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 11. Appropriate for General Stabilization Fund (Board of Selectmen) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money to the General Stabilization Fund in accordance with Chapter 40, Section 5B of the Massachusetts General Laws; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 12.
