On request of the Select Board. RECOMMENDATION (Finance Committee): That the sum of $16,700,000 is appropriated to pay costs of the demolition of the existing East Falmouth Branch Library and to pay costs of design and construction of a new library at the existing site located at 310 East Falmouth Highway including, without limitation, landscaping, paving, utility and other site improvements, storage and moving expenses, furnishings and equipment and all other costs incidental or related thereto; to authorize the Town to accept and expend any grants, donations, or loans available for the project, including the Massachusetts Board of Library Commissioners grant; and to meet this appropriation, the Treasurer with the approval of the Select Board, is authorized to borrow said amount under and pursuant to Chapter 44, Section 7 (1) of the Mass. General Laws, or pursuant to any other enabling authority, and to issue bonds or notes of the Town therefor. No sums shall be borrowed or expended hereunder unless and until the Town shall have voted to exclude the amounts required to repay any borrowing authorized by this vote from the limitations of Chapter 59, Section 21C of the Mass. General Laws (also known as Proposition 2½), said funds to be expended under the jurisdiction of the Town Manager. EXPLANATION: The existing East Falmouth Branch Library was originally constructed as a single-family house. A building assessment prepared by Gale Associates estimated the cost of repairs required to address immediate structural and water infiltration issues, bring the building up to code, and extend the useful life of the structure at $3.4 million of which $2.1 million is recommended to be completed right away. These repairs would not provide any added program space or a community meeting room. Based on this study and community input, the Falmouth Public Library Board of Trustees and the Select Board determined that renovation of the existing structure is not a viable option. The Town has secured a grant from the Massachusetts Board of Library Commissioners in the amount of $7,194,749 to construct a new library on the existing site. This grant opportunity is only made available by the state every five years or so. The cost to Falmouth taxpayers will be further offset by generous donations from three library support groups (i.e. Library Board of Trustees, Friends of Falmouth Public Library, Falmouth Public Library Support Fund) who have pledged a combined total of $3 million to support this project with funds already on deposit. The estimated net cost to taxpayers is $6,505,251 for total remaining project costs including all soft costs, furnishing and equipment. The annual debt service is estimated to be $399,659 per year based on a 30year, level debt bond with a 4.5% interest rate. Based on these estimates, this project will result in a temporary tax impact for 30 years of approximately 2 cents on the tax rate. The estimated impact on the median single-family house with a value of $791,800 based on the FY2026 actual tax levy and tax rate would be $15.84 per year. ARTICLE 10: To see if the Town will vote to amend the Code of Falmouth, Section 107, Demolition Delay, by deleting portions of certain sections and inserting new provisions. The deletions are illustrated below by strikethrough and the insertions are illustrated in bold as follows: Demolition Delay PRESERVATION OF SIGNIFICANT BUILDINGS § 107-1. Intent and purpose. This bylaw is enacted for the purpose of preserving and protecting designated significant buildings within the Town which constitute or reflect distinctive features of the architectural, cultural, economic, political or social history of the Town and to limit the detrimental effect of demolition on the character of the Town. Through this bylaw, owners of significant buildings determined to be significant by the Historical Commission are encouraged to seek out alternatives to demolition that will preserve, rehabilitate or restore such buildings, and residents of the Town are alerted to impending demolitions of significant buildings. By preserving and protecting significant buildings, and the streetscapes and neighborhoods they form, this bylaw makes the Town a more attractive and desirable place in which to live and work. To achieve these purposes and thereby promote the public welfare, the Historical Commission is authorized to advise the Building Commissioner with respect to demolition permit applications. The issuance of demolition permits is regulated as provided by this bylaw. § 107-2. Definitions. As used in this article, the following terms shall have the meanings indicated: ADVISORY REVIEW — A discussion by the Historical Commission with the applicant of why the building should be preserved and ways to avoid demolition. The purpose of the advisory review is to allow the Historical Commission to assist and encourage the applicant to seek out alternatives to demolition that will preserve, rehabilitate or restore the building, or if demolition is to proceed to provide suitable documentation of the building for the permanent records of the Commission. APPLICANT — Any person or entity who files an application for, or a request for review of demolition relative to, a demolition permit with the Building Commissioner. If the applicant is not the owner of the premises upon which the building is situated to be demolished, the owner must indicate on or with the application must include written his/her assent of the owner to the filing of the application. Failure to provide such assent will render the application incomplete. APPLICATION — An application for the demolition of a building. BUILDING — Any combination of materials forming a shelter for persons, animals, or property. BUILDING COMMISSIONER — The person occupying the office of Building Commissioner or otherwise authorized to issue demolition permits. COMMISSION — The Falmouth Historical Commission or its designee. DEMOLITION — Any act of pulling down, destroying, removing, dismantling or razing a building or commencing the work of total or substantial destruction with the intent of completing the same. DEMOLITION PERMIT — The building permit issued by the Building Inspector for a demolition of a building, excluding a building permit issued solely for the demolition of the interior of a building. LETTER OF CERTIFICATION — A letter from the Town Clerk noting the date on which a request for review of demolition has been recorded and indicating whether the building is on the List of Significant Buildings. The Town Clerk shall send this letter to the Building Commissioner and the Historical Commission with a copy of the request for review of demolition. LIST OF SIGNIFICANT BUILDINGS — A list, to be created by the Historical Commission and kept by the Town Clerk, of significant buildings as determined according to the provisions of this article. (See "significant building.") SIGNIFICANT BUILDING — Any building within the Town, but not within a Local Historic District, which is at least 50 years old in whole or in part, and meets at least one of the following criteria as has been determined by the Commission, according to the provisions of this article, to be significant based on any of the following criteria: A. The building is listed on, or is within an area listed on, the National or State Register of Historic Places; or B. The building has been found eligible for the National or State Register of Historic Places; or C. The building is importantly associated with one or more historic persons or events, or with the broad architectural, cultural, political, economic or social history of the Town or the commonwealth; or D. It should take less than five minutes of your time. ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS FRANKLIN, SS. TOWN OF GILL ANNUAL TOWN MEETING: MAY 4, 2026 To any of the Constables of the Town of Gill in the County of Franklin, Greetings: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of said town, qualified to vote in elections and in town affairs, to meet at the Gill Town Hall, 325 Main Road in said town on Monday, the Fourth day of May, in the year Two Thousand and Twenty Six (05/04/2026) at 7:00 PM then and there to act on the following articles. Article 1: To elect the following officers: Two or more Field Drivers; Fence Viewers; Measurers of Wood, Bark and Surveyors of Lumber - all for one year; AND To see if the Town will vote to accept and expend any sum of money that might be made available from State or Federal funds for roadwork or other purposes for the Fiscal Year 2027 and for the Chapter 90 type funds, authorize the Selectboard to enter into contracts with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts Department of Transportation; AND To see if the Town will vote to accept any sum of money that might be made available from the Quintus Allen Trust during Fiscal Year 2027, and authorize the Selectboard to expend such funds in support of the Gill Elementary School, or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to elect Edward J. Golembeski and Clifford C. Hatch as Field Drivers and the Regional Animal Control Officer as Assistant Field Driver and elect the Selectboard as Fence Viewers; Measurers of Wood, Bark and Surveyors of Lumber - all for one year; AND It is moved the Town vote to accept and expend any sum of money that might be made available from State or Federal funds for roadwork or other purposes for the Fiscal Year 2027 and for the Chapter 90 type funds, authorize the Selectboard to enter into contracts with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts Department of Transportation; AND It is moved the Town vote to accept any sum of money that might be made available from the Quintus Allen Trust during Fiscal Year 2027, and authorize the Selectboard to expend such funds in support of the Gill Elementary School. The Finance Committee voted to recommend this article by a vote of 5 in favor and 0 opposed. The names and positions (Field Drivers, Fence Viewers, and etc.) are the same as last year. Chapter 90 funds are given annually by the state to the Town and are used for our road maintenance program – activities such as repaving asphalt roads, applying new oil & stone (now called “chip sealing”), and drainage and guardrail projects. In Fiscal Years 2024 and 2025 the state also provided Chapter 90like funds for road maintenance through the Rural Roads and the Fair Share programs. The total state aid received in Fiscal Year 2024 was $351,059, and $289,742 was received in Fiscal Year 2025. For Fiscal Year 2025 the Town anticipates it will receive $260,781 through the Chapter 90 program plus an additional $75,009 from a supplemental Chapter 90 appropriation, for a total of $335,790. Subject to approval by the Legislature, the Town expects to receive $260,000 of traditional Chapter 90 funds for Fiscal Year 2027, and it is too soon to know if there will be any supplemental allocations. And while $260K is a lot of money, keep in mind the estimated cost to mill and re-pave 1.5 miles of West Gill Road last year was $288,000. Gill has approximately 26 miles of paved roads and 8.5 miles of gravel roads. Quintus Allen was an original trustee of the Greenfield Savings Bank. Upon his death in 1884, his will established a trust fund to be used for education-related expenses in Colrain, Gill, Leyden, and Shelburne. The interest earned by the Trust is distributed to those towns each year. The Town received $2,459 from the Trust during Fiscal Year 2026, and there is a balance of $10,009 in the Town’s Quintus Allen account. In response to a shortage of homes and skyrocketing housing prices in Massachusetts, the Affordable Homes Act was enacted in August 2024. A key provision of the law is that it supersedes local zoning bylaws and allows ADUs “by right” (without a zoning special permit) on any lot with a pre-existing home. ADUs must still adhere to building and fire codes and must follow Title 5 septic regulations. Towns are allowed to regulate ADUs but may not be more restrictive than the state’s regulations. Highlights of Gill’s proposed zoning bylaw on ADUs include: a higher maximum square footage (up to 1,200 sq ft) for an ADU in all areas of town except the Village Residential zoning district (Riverside, essentially); ADUs may not be used as short-term rentals (i.e. AirBNB); and ADUs must be located within 100 feet of the principal dwelling. TOWN OF GILL ANNUAL TOWN MEETING: MAY 4, 2026 To any of the Constables of the Town of Gill in the County of Franklin, Greetings: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of said town, qualified to vote in elections and in town affairs, to meet at the Gill Town Hall, 325 Main Road in said town on Monday, the Fourth day of May, in the year Two Thousand and Twenty Six (05/04/2026) at 7:00 PM then and there to act on the following articles. ~~~ The town meeting on Monday, June 8, 2026, at 7:00 PM at the Town Hall is a continuation of the Annual Town Meeting originally opened on Monday, May 4, 2026. Articles 1 through 7 were addressed on May 4 th. The motions and explanations for those articles have been omitted from this handout to reduce printing costs. ~~~ Article 8 (Compensation for Town Officers): To see if the Town will vote to fix the salaries or compensation of the several officers of the Town as follows, or take any action relative thereto. *Constable(s) – Each Posting *Moderator – Annual Town Meeting Special Town Meeting, Each *Selectboard Chair 2nd & 3rd Member, Each *Board of Assessors Chair 2nd & 3rd Member, Each *Board of Health Chair 2nd & 3rd Member, Each Town Clerk Registrars – Three members, Each Town Clerk, as Chair $22.00 $152.00 $28.00 $2,778.00 $2,525.00 $3,374.00 $3,067.00 $1,522.00 $1,393.00 $30,486.00 $73.00 $118.00 Motion: It is moved the Town vote to fix the salaries or compensation of the several officers of the Town as listed in the Article, plus any cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) and/or any Wage Compensation Plan updates that may be provided by the Town. The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 5 in favor and 0 opposed. All amounts are level funded (with rounding) from Fiscal Year 2026. A COLA, if approved in Article 10, would be in addition to the amounts listed above. The elected positions preceded by an asterisk (*) are not included in the COLA proposed in Article 10 on the basis the provided stipends are more akin to honorariums and are not intended to be working wages compensation for the time spent on the duties of the positions. The Town Clerk is the only position listed above affected by the funding requested in Article 9 to implement updates to the Wage Compensation Plan. As an elected position, the Town Clerk is not included in the Wage Compensation Plan, however, for purposes of comparison and fair compensation, the position was included in an outside analysis of the Town’s compensation that was conducted last year. The vote of Town Meeting will continue to be the way the Town Clerk’s compensation is set. If Articles 9 and 10 are both approved, the Town Clerk’s total compensation will be $32,403. Article 9 (Funds to Implement Changes to Wage Compensation Plan): To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate by taxation, transfer from available funds or otherwise provide a sum or sums of money to implement Annual Town Meeting – Part 2 – June 8, 2026 Page 1 of 8 updates to the Town’s Wage Compensation Plan as recommended by the Personnel Committee and Selectboard, or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to raise and appropriate by taxation $21,300.00 to implement updates to the Town’s Wage Compensation Plan as recommended by the Personnel Committee and Selectboard. The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 4 in favor, 0 opposed, and 1 recused. The Town of Gill's current wage scale is at least 20-25 years old, as is the classification system used to rank and place positions on the wage scale. The methodology is outdated, and job descriptions have not been kept current or standardized, largely due to relatively low turnover rates and an all-volunteer Personnel Committee. The wage scale has increased by an average of 2.46% annually for the past 20 years. Despite this, the entire first level and one-third of the second level of our existing wage scale is below the Massachusetts minimum wage of $16/hour. In the last 5 years when the Town has recruited and hired personnel we have often needed to start new hires possessing entry-level experience at the second or third step on the wage scale (which would take two to four years to reach as an employee) in order to be competitive with other towns in our area and, for positions requiring a CDL license, with the private sector as well. When other towns in our region advertise their vacancies, the starting wages are frequently significantly higher than ours for the equivalent position. Recognizing we were overdue for an update to our job descriptions, classification system, and wage scale, the Town applied for and received a $13,000 award from the State’s Community Compact Cabinet to hire the Collins Center for Public Management to perform a Classification and Compensation Study. This work was completed in 2025, but too late to be implemented in Fiscal Year 2026. The Personnel Committee has completed its review of the proposed wage scale, although it is continuing to work on fine-tuning and finalizing the job descriptions. The remaining work on the job descriptions is not believed to have an impact on positions’ placement on the new wage scale. The current wage scale has 8 grades, and each grade has 6 steps. Typically, an employee will start on the first step, move up one step for every 2 years of employment, and reach the last step during their 11th year of employment. The new wage scale has 6 grades, and each grade has 10 steps. Employees will move up one step for each year of employment, reaching the last step during their 10 th year of employment. According to the Personnel Policy, it is the Selectboard’s responsibility to adopt changes to the wage compensation plan. However, when those changes have a financial impact, Town Meeting must appropriate the funds to implement the changes. In determining the cost to implement the new wage compensation plan, the current wage scale was used to determine each employee’s wage rate effective on July 1, 2026, the start of Fiscal Year 2027. Then, from the appropriate grade level on the new wage scale, each employee was assigned a wage rate that is equal to or greater than the rate from the current wage scale (i.e. no employee will earn a lower rate because of the new wage scale). The estimated annual wages for each employee was calculated using the rates from the current and new wage scales, and the difference is the amount requested in Article 9. Article 10 (COLA for Town Employees): To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate by taxation a sum or sums of money to provide a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for all appointed Town employees and certain elected officials, or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to raise and appropriate by taxation $24,200.00 to provide a 2% cost-ofliving adjustment (COLA) for the Police Chief and a 3% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for all other appointed Town employees and the elected Town Clerk. The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 4 in favor, 0 opposed, and 1 recused. The proposed 3% COLA for Fiscal Year 2027 is slightly higher than the 2.8% increase provided to Social Security recipients effective in January 2026 and the 2.9% increase indicated by the Consumer Price Index. In recommending the higher amount the Personnel Committee noted 1) the importance of keeping pace with inflation, and 2) the need to offset an almost 60% increase in the cost of employee’s health insurance from Fiscal Year 2025 to Fiscal Year 2027. Annual Town Meeting – Part 2 – June 8, 2026 Page 2 of 8 The Police Chief’s most recent employment contract, covering Fiscal Years 2026 through 2028, includes a clause by which any COLA increase to his salary must be proposed and approved by a majority vote of the Selectboard. At its June 1, 2026 meeting the Selectboard voted the 2% COLA for the Police Chief, noting the first year of the current contract included a significant increase to the Chief’s salary. Certain elected positions (Constables, Moderator, Selectboard members, Assessors, and Board of Health members) are excluded from this COLA on the basis the provided stipends are more akin to honorariums, and are not intended to be working wages compensation for the time spent on the duties of the positions. Article 11 (Omnibus Budget): To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate by taxation, transfer from available funds or otherwise provide a sum or sums of money for the maintenance of the several departments of the Town (the “Omnibus budget”) for Fiscal Year 2027, and for other necessary charges, in accordance with the amounts recommended by the Selectboard, or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to raise and appropriate by taxation $2,228,405.00 and transfer $110,000.00 from Sewer Use Fees and appropriate $82,500.00 from Fiscal Year 2027 Estimated Sewer Receipts and transfer $11,967.00 from the Energy Stabilization Fund and transfer $222,000.00 from the General Stabilization Fund for a total appropriation of $2,654,872.00 for the maintenance of the several departments of the Town (the “Omnibus budget”) for Fiscal Year 2027, and for other necessary charges, in accordance with the amount recommended by the Selectboard. A 2/3 majority is needed to transfer funds out of the Energy Stabilization Fund and the General Stabilization Fund. The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 4 in favor and 1 opposed. Please see the separate handout (legal-sized paper) for the Omnibus amounts and accompanying notes. The amounts in the motion come from page 3, Column D, lines 88 – 94 of the handout. The second sheet of this stapled handout contains general remarks about financial challenges faced in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget. As of May 31, 2026, and excluding any amounts approved to be used in other articles voted tonight, the Energy Stabilization Fund had a balance of $43,089 and the General Stabilization Fund had a balance of $649,511. A complete list of the Town’s stabilization funds and balances can be found in the explanation for Article 20. This use of stabilization is unprecedented, at least within the past several decades. The costs of necessary services in next year’s budget have risen faster than the Town’s revenues available to pay for them. Among the cost drivers are health insurance, school assessments, and the ripple-through effects of elevated costs of diesel fuel, gasoline, and heating oil. In building the budget for Fiscal Year 2027 the Town departments presented the minimum budgets required to continue the services residents require and expect, and the Selectboard and Finance Committee scrutinized department budget requests for ways to trim costs. The other unusual twist to this year’s budget discussions was the lack of certified Free Cash to use for one-time expenses (Articles 15, 18, and 19) and to reduce next year’s tax rate and stabilize the tax levy (Article 21). Normally, by the time Annual Town Meeting is held, the Town’s Free Cash from the prior year (Fiscal Year 2025) has been certified by the Department of Revenue. Gill’s Free Cash has not been submitted for certification yet due to extra time required to reconcile the Accountant’s figures with those of the Treasurer (cash book) and the previous Collector (tax payments), coupled with the steep learning curve for someone still relatively new to the Town Accountant role. We anticipate Free Cash will be submitted and certified in time for a Special Town Meeting on June 29th, at which time most or all of the Free Cash is likely to be recommended to be voted into the various stabilization funds. A Proposition 2 ½ override was seriously considered and the ballot vote was even scheduled for June 15th. However, after extensive discussions the Selectboard and Finance Committee decided the Town’s fiscal reserves (stabilization funds) were adequate and could be used without detrimental impact. One reason for placing money into stabilization funds is to have reserves to use in the event of a financial “rainy day.” The Fiscal Year 2027 budget is certainly a “rainy day.” The June 15th vote has been cancelled. Annual Town Meeting – Part 2 – June 8, 2026 Page 3 of 8 The use of $11,967 from the Energy Stabilization Fund will cover the next-to-last year of the Town’s payments for the bond (loan) taken out in 2012 as part of an energy conservation project at the Elementary School that included a new boiler, a building energy management system, and lighting upgrades. Roughly $18,000 of the $43,089 currently in the Energy Stabilization Fund was due to energy savings realized by the GMRSD in the early years after the equipment was installed and returned to the Town to help pay for the project. Article 12 (GMRSD Assessment): To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate by taxation, transfer from available funds or otherwise provide $2,149,571.00 for its Fiscal Year 2027 operating assessment for the GillMontague Regional School District, or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to raise and appropriate by taxation $2,057,571.00 and further transfer $92,000.00 from the Education Stabilization Fund to provide $2,149,571.00 for its Fiscal Year 2027 operating assessment for the Gill-Montague Regional School District (GMRSD). A 2/3 majority is needed to transfer funds out of the Education Stabilization Fund. The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 5 in favor and 0 opposed. A handout from the GMRSD is attached (blue paper, immediately after the legal-sized paper in this handout), and District officials are in attendance to answer questions. The GMRSD’s total Fiscal Year 2027 “All Funds” budget increased by 3.1% over Fiscal Year 2026. Gill’s assessment for the GMRSD’s operating budget increased by $163,760 (8.2%), driven partly by an increase in the Required Minimum Contribution calculated by the State and partly by enrollment changes of the two towns. There are no debt service costs for the high school/middle school renovation project, as the loan for that project was paid off this year. Gill’s enrollment in the District decreased 3.2% from 93 to 90 students at the same time Montague’s enrollment decreased 5.0% from 637 to 605. Gill’s share of the District’s operating costs increased from 12.74% to 12.95% and Montague’s share decreased from 87.26% to 87.05%. “Putting money into the Education Stabilization Fund provides a reserve that can be used in future years in the event of a significant increase in assessments or other educational needs.” This statement has appeared in many of the recent Town Meeting handouts as part of the explanation for the Article related to adding funds to the Town’s various Stabilization Funds. Gill’s Fiscal Year 2027 assessments for the GMRSD ($163,760 increase) and the Franklin County Technical School ($17,348 decrease) have a net increase of $146,412 (6.6%) over the Fiscal Year 2026 assessments. The Selectboard and Finance Committee agreed this is a “significant increase” and are recommending using $92,000 from the Education Stabilization Fund to mitigate the need for a Proposition 2-1/2 Override vote. The balance in the Education Stabilization Fund as of May 31, 2026, was $287,542. Article 13 (Assessors’ Utility Appraisals): To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate by taxation, transfer from available funds or otherwise provide a sum or sums of money to add to the account to be used toward the costs associated with an appraisal of the real and personal property in the Town of Gill owned by FirstLight Power and Northfield Mountain LLC and an appraisal of the personal property in the Town of Gill owned by National Grid, New England Power Company, and NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to raise and appropriate by taxation $4,000.00 to add to the account to be used toward the costs associated with an appraisal of the real and personal property in the Town of Gill owned by FirstLight Power and Northfield Mountain LLC and appraisals of the personal property in the Town of Gill owned by National Grid, New England Power Company, and NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy. The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 5 in favor and 0 opposed. In October 2025, after receiving approval from Town Meeting, the Town signed a payment-in-lieu-oftaxes (PILOT) agreement with FirstLight Power for the Turners Falls Dam and related assets and parcels of land. An appraisal of the dam will not be required for 10 years. However, in 2026, as part of the Fiscal Year 2027 recertification of property values and assessments by the Department of Revenue (DOR), the Assessors are being required to obtain an appraisal of the value of the Gill portion of FirstLight’s Northfield Mountain pumped storage hydroelectric facility and related assets and parcels of land. Gill Annual Town Meeting – Part 2 – June 8, 2026 Page 4 of 8 will share the cost of this appraisal with the Towns of Erving and Northfield. Yearly appraisals are also needed to substantiate the valuation of the several electricity distribution companies with property in Gill. This article adds to the existing account, and funds will be used for the appraisals required for the Fiscal Year 2027 recertification. Any unspent money will be saved toward interim year appraisals and updates next year. Article 14 (Assessors’ Revaluation): To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate by taxation, transfer from available funds or otherwise provide a sum or sums of money to add to the Board of Assessors Revaluation Account (001-142-5801), or take any action relative thereto. Motion: It is moved the Town vote to raise and appropriate by taxation $3,000.00 to add to the Board of Assessors’ Revaluation Account (001-142-5801). The Finance Committee recommends this article by a vote of 5 in favor and 0 opposed. Fiscal Year 2027 is the next recertification year for Gill, in which the Department of Revenue will review and certify property values town wide. Because of the added level of research and analysis, the Assessors incur extra costs during revaluation years. This article adds money to the Revaluation Account to ensure there are adequate funds for this year’s revaluation work. Any unspent money will be saved toward the next recertification in 2032. Article 1 (Adding to OPEB Fund): To see if the Town will vote to transfer from unappropriated funds (Free Cash) or other available funds or otherwise provide a sum or sums of money for the Other Post-Employment Benefits Liability Trust Fund, or take any action relative thereto. title: Explanation of Warrant Articles - 2026 Annual Town Meeting Warrant
text: May 11, 2026 – 6:30 pm TOWN OF HAMPDEN SPRING ANNUAL TOWN MEETING EXPLANATIONS AND BACKGROUND INFORMATION Disclaimer: The amounts, if any, listed below for each article are estimates and are subject to change. If there is any discrepancy between the warrant article or a motion made during the Town Meeting and this document then the warrant article/motion controls. For this Town Meeting, the Moderator will be implementing a procedure known as the Consent Agenda. The Consent Agenda is a process through which non-controversial and housekeeping type articles are voted on with a single motion. The purpose of the Consent Agenda is to save time as it disposes of the need to read a motion for and vote on each of the articles separately. Any registered voter may voice an objection and request that the Moderator remove the article from the Consent Agenda. Any articles removed from the Consent Agenda will be considered in the normal order of business. For the upcoming Spring Annual Town Meeting the first four (4) articles are identified as Consent Agenda articles. Consent Agenda articles are designated with the (+CA) symbol on the warrant. ***Begin Consent Agenda*** Article 1. Town Reports (+CA): This standard article requests that voters hear the Annual Reports of all officers and committees of the Town. No funds requested. Article 2. FY 2027 Spending Limits for Revolving Funds (+CA): This standard article requests that voters set the spending limits for pre-existing revolving funds. Revolving funds are separate accounts from which specific revenue is received and certain expenses are paid. The revolving funds are established through the Town’s General Bylaws. State law requires that spending limits for the revolving funds be voted each fiscal year. This article does not raise and appropriate any money instead it simply sets a maximum amount that the Department can spend from the account identified. No funds requested. 1 May 11, 2026 – 6:30 pm Article 3. Library Additional State Aid (+CA): This standard article requests that voters agree to accept the annual library funding from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. For informational purposes, Hampden’s library received $14,160 in state aid from the Commonwealth for fiscal year 2026. No funds requested. Article 4. Assessor’s Funding for State Mandated Programs (+CA): This article requests that voters agree to raise and appropriate money for the purpose of paying costs for activities mandated by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue (e.g. required inspections and property valuations). The estimated funding request for this article is $18,000. ***End Consent Agenda*** Article 5. Report of the Old Town House Committee: This article requests voters agree to hear a report from the Old Town House Committee. The Old Town House Committee was established in December 2025 to study and explore future scenarios for the now vacant and underutilized Town House located at 625 Main Street. No funds requested. Article 6. Chapter 90: State Highway Aid: This standard article requests that voters agree to accept the annual highway funding from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, commonly known as Chapter 90 funds. Hampden’s estimated Chapter 90 allotment for fiscal year 2027 is $428,221.88. No funds requested. Article 7. Annual Operating Budget: This article requests that voters approve the annual operating budget as recommended by the Advisory Committee. The budget recommendations from the Advisory Committee can be found on the Green Sheets. Copies of the Green Sheets can be found on the Town’s website (www.hampdenma.gov) and will be mailed out in the Wilbraham Hampden Times. The recommended annual operating budget from the Advisory Committee is $18,600,891. Please see the Green Sheets for more details. 2 May 11, 2026 – 6:30 pm Article 8. Hampden Wilbraham Regional School District Capital Assessment: This article requests that voters approve the capital assessment for the Hampden Wilbraham Regional School District as proposed by the School Committee. The Town of Hampden’s share of the proposed HWRSD capital assessment is $34,652. The total proposed capital assessment for Wilbraham is $135,348 for a total request of $170,000. The proposed capital assessment will pay for the purchase and installation of IDF switches and network upgrades and the purchase of a dump body truck/sander. The estimated funding request for this article is $34,652. Article 9. Enterprise Fund: Transfer Station: This article requests that voters approve the annual budget for the Transfer Station Enterprise Fund and to raise and appropriate an additional amount of funds to supplement the Transfer Station operations. An enterprise fund is a separate account from which specific revenue is received and certain expenses are paid from, similar to a revolving fund, except that any annual surplus funds carry over to the next fiscal year as retained earnings and remain in the enterprise fund account. The annual operating budget for the transfer station is estimated to be $146,500 with $131,500 raised from transfer station receipts and the remaining $15,000 from raise and appropriate. Article 10. Funding for Hampden’s 150th Anniversary Events: Hampden turns 150 years old in 2028. This article requests that voters approve a sum of money to be set aside to pay for future costs associated with the celebration of the Town’s 150th anniversary. To date, $20,000 has been set aside for this celebration. No funds requested. The anticipated motion is to take no action on this article. Article 11. School Resource Officer – Minnechaug Regional H.S.: This article requests that voters approve a sum of money to pay for the shared cost of having a school resource officer at Minnechaug Regional High School. The costs for this position are shared between Hampden and Wilbraham, with Hampden contributing 20.93% of the total cost of the school resource officer. The estimated funding request for this article is $14,210. Article 12. Prior Year Bills: This article requests that voters approve a sum of money to pay for costs and expenses incurred during a previous fiscal year. State law provides that the expenses of a prior fiscal year can only be paid upon approval by 9/10ths of voters at a Town Meeting. At the time of the writing of this document, there are no known prior year expenses that need approval. No funds requested. 3 May 11, 2026 – 6:30 pm Article 13. Community Preservation Committee: A. This article requests that voters approve a sum of money from the Community Preservation Fund for the rehabilitation of Niccum Field at Memorial Park. The proposed work at Niccum Field (baseball field) is to reconstruct and grade the infield playing surface through laser leveling. The estimated funding request for this article is $25,000 from the Community Preservation Fund. B. This article requests that voters approve a sum of money from the Community Preservation Fund for the purchase of an approximately 18.36-acre lot located on the south side of the Scantic River off Main Street, for open space and conservation purposes and to also convey a conservation restriction on said lot to the Minnechaug Land Trust or other qualified organizations. Please see Attachment A to the Annual Town Meeting warrant for a map showing the lot proposed for acquisition. The estimated funding request for this article is $60,000 from the Community Preservation Fund. The purchase price of the property will not exceed $40,000 and the remaining up to $20,000 will be available for due diligence and closing costs. Article 14: Repeal Community Preservation Act: This article presents voters with an opportunity to vote to repeal the Community Preservation Act (CPA). Hampden adopted the CPA in 2001, which adds a 1% surcharge to the tax bill of residents. The amount raised through the CPA surcharge is deposited into the Community Preservation Fund and can only be spent on qualifying projects that support housing, historic preservation, open space and recreation. The Commonwealth of Massachusetts provides matching funds each fiscal year to municipalities that have adopted the CPA. The amount of matching funds varies each year in accordance with a funding formula. For example, in fiscal year 2025, Hampden generated $100,996 from the CPA surcharge and the Commonwealth paid to Hampden an additional $16,730 in matching CPA funds. Please know that to repeal the CPA, residents must vote in favor of repeal at the Town Meeting and then again vote in favor of repeal at the upcoming election in November 2026. If the repeal effort is successful, the repeal will likely come into effect starting fiscal year 2028. No funds requested 4 May 11, 2026 – 6:30 pm Article 15. Recission of Prior Appropriation for Purchase of Approximately 2.1 Acres of Land on North Road: This article asks voters to rescind a previous appropriation of Community Preservation Act funds for the purchase of a 2.1 2.1-acre (Lot B-R) on North Road for conservation purposes. The Minnechaug Land Trust purchased an approximately 4acre parcel and split the large parcel into two 2-acres parcels. The Town had previously voted to acquire lot B-R from the Minnechaug Land Trust to establish a parking area and trail head to access the hiking trails on Mount Vision. Minnechaug Land Trust intended to sell the remaining lot (Lot A-R) as a building lot but ran into difficulties with site constraints. Minnechaug Land Trust is now proposing that the Town purchase the former Lot A-R instead of the former lot B-R. The proposed vote to rescind the approval under this article and the proposed vote in the next article will accomplish that. Please see Attachment B to the Annual Town Meeting warrant for a map showing the lot proposed for acquisition. No funds requested. This article requests that $95,000 be returned to the Community Preservation Fund. Article 16. Purchase of Approximately 2.676 Acres of Land on North Road: This article requests that voters authorize the Selectboard to purchase a 2.676-acre parcel of land on North Road for open space purposes and the construction of a small parking area and trail head to provide public access to the hiking trails on Mount Vision and to also convey a conservation restriction on said lot to the Minnechaug Land Trust or other qualified organizations. Please see the explanation for Article 15 above. The estimated funding request for this article is $95,000 from the Community Preservation Fund. Article 17. Amendment to the Posting Location of Town Meeting Warrants: This article requests that voters approve an amendment to the Town’s General Bylaws to add the bulletin board outside the new Town Hall located at 85 Wilbraham Road as a required posting location of the Town Meeting warrants and to remove the bulletin board outside the old Town House (625 Main Street) as a required posting location. In November 2025, all municipal offices and the library moved to the new Town Hall leaving the old Town House vacant. No funds requested. Article 18. Advisory Committee Reserve Fund: This article requests that voters approve a sum of money to be placed into a reserve fund, under the control of the Advisory Committee, to pay for extraordinary and unforeseen expenses that may arise during fiscal year 2027. The estimated funding request for this article will range between $10,000 to $25,000. 5 May 11, 2026 – 6:30 pm Article 19. General Stabilization Fund: This article requests that voters approve a sum of money to be placed into the General Stabilization Fund (savings account) for future town expenses. The use of any money from the General Stabilization Fund requires approval of voters at a future Town Meeting. The estimated funding request for this article is to be determined. Article 20. Reducing the Tax Rate: This article requests that voters approve a sum of money to reduce the amount of the tax levy for fiscal year 2026. Voters have the option of using available funds (savings) to pay for the operating expenses of the Town. Using available funds to pay for operating expenses reduces the tax burden on residents for the upcoming fiscal year. As a matter of practice, voters are asked to consider this article during the Fall Town Meeting once the previous fiscal year has closed and Free Cash has been certified by the Commonwealth. The estimated funding request for this article is to be determined. 6

text: TOWN OF HINGHAM WARRANT for the SPECIAL TOWN MEETING Thursday, October 29, 2026 at 7:00 P.M. Hingham High School 17 Union Street, Hingham, MA Please bring this report to the meeting for use in the proceedings TABLE OF CONTENTS Page 2 Town Meeting Procedures 20 Municipal Finance Terms 21 Talent Bank Application Special Town Election 4 Page Call of Town Meeting and Town Election Article Special Town Meeting Articles 5 1 South Elementary School Roof 10 2 Plymouth River Elementary School Roof 15 3 High School Roof and HVAC Design 1 MODERATOR'S MESSAGE ON TOWN MEETING PROCEDURES Welcome to the 2026 Hingham Special Town Meeting. In our commitment to open town meeting, Hingham remains true to a wonderful tradition – a tradition that allows each registered voter to play a pivotal role in the governance of the town and to do so with “voice and vote”. Town meeting is not only a gathering of citizens to consider matters of common concern; it is the legislative body of the town. As such, the meeting must be conducted in a fair and open manner and in accordance with the Town Bylaws, as well as traditions that we have followed in Hingham town meetings for many years. Several matters of procedure are summarized below.  An article in the warrant states a question for the town meeting to answer. A motion is a proposed answer to the question and must be within the scope of the article. An article (once published in the warrant) may not be amended, but a motion may be amended by vote of the meeting. All motions must be seconded.  If the Advisory Committee is recommending an affirmative motion under an article, its motion will be received as the main motion under the article. A voter may propose to amend this motion, either to change it in part or to substitute a whole new motion (sometimes called a "substitute motion"). In any such case, the proposed amendment will be taken up and voted on first and then the main motion, as it may have been amended, will be acted upon.  If the Advisory Committee is recommending no action under an article and a voter offers an affirmative motion, the voter's motion will be received as the main motion under the article. Such a motion is likewise subject to amendment.  All motions and proposed amendments involving the expenditure of money must be in writing. So must all other motions and proposed amendments unless they are so brief and simple as to be easily understood when stated orally (e.g., motion for the previous question, motion to adjourn). Voters are welcome to seek the assistance of counsel for the Town in preparing motions or proposed amendments.  Limits on speaking: No one may speak on any subject for more than six (6) minutes for the first time or for more than three (3) minutes for the second time. No one may speak more than twice on any question unless all others who have not spoken on the question shall have spoken if they desire to do so and unless leave of the meeting is first obtained. A person may speak more than twice, but only to make a brief correction of an error in or misunderstanding of his or her previous statement, including brief answers to questions from the floor (addressed through the Moderator).  In addressing the meeting, a speaker shall confine his or her remarks to the matter before the meeting.  Persons who are not registered voters of the Town may be admitted to the meeting as guests by the Moderator. A guest of the meeting may be granted permission to address the meeting by majority vote.  The purpose of the motion for the previous question is to end discussion and have an immediate vote on the pending question. The motion is not debatable and requires a majority vote for adoption. The Moderator will decline to accept a motion for the previous question if 2 other voters are seeking recognition and if both sides have not had a fair opportunity to be heard. The Moderator will accept the motion for the previous question if it appears that both sides have been heard and the discussion is becoming repetitious.  Voting procedures: All votes are taken in the first instance by voice vote. If the Moderator is in doubt as to the results or if seven (7) voters rise and express doubt as to the result declared by the Moderator, a standing vote is taken, except that a ballot vote is taken (instead of a standing vote) if either the Advisory Committee or fifty (50) voters promptly call for a ballot vote. As a ballot vote takes considerable time, our practice has been not to request a ballot vote in the absence of compelling reasons.  At a Special Town Meeting, no money may be appropriated for any purpose if the Advisory Committee recommends against the appropriation, except by a two-thirds vote of the meeting.  No vote may be reconsidered except after a two-thirds vote on a motion to reconsider such vote. A vote may not be reconsidered a second time or after a motion to reconsider it has failed to pass.  A vote adopted at one session of the town meeting may not be reconsidered at a later (adjourned) session of the meeting unless the mover has given notice of the mover’s intention to make such a motion either at the session of the meeting at which the vote was passed or by written notice to the Town Clerk not less than 12 hours before the hour to which adjournment has been voted and not more than 48 hours after the hour of adjournment of such session. Any motion for reconsideration pursuant to such notice of intention will be taken up at the beginning of the adjourned session.  Articles in the warrant are to be acted upon in their order unless the meeting otherwise determines by majority vote.  A motion to adjourn the meeting to a later time is a privileged motion and is decided by majority vote without debate. When the warrant is completed, a motion to dissolve the meeting is in order.  The number of voters constituting a quorum in order to convene the first session of a Regular or Special Town Meeting is 300. The number of voters necessary to convene the second or any subsequent session of a Regular or Special Town Meeting is 200. Once convened, the quorum to transaction business at any Regular or Special Town Meeting is 200; provided, however, that a number of less than 200 may from time to time adjourn the same. Once a quorum is determined at the start of the meeting (or adjourned session), the presence of a quorum is presumed to continue unless a point of no quorum is raised and a count of the meeting shows that a quorum is not present. In that event, the meeting may be adjourned to a later date.  If you wish to speak, please rise and seek the attention of the Moderator or the Assistant Moderator. When recognized by the Moderator, you should come to a microphone. Please state your name and address at the outset each time you speak. Michael J. Puzo Moderator October 2026 3 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS Plymouth, ss. To the Constables of the Town of Hingham in the County of Plymouth, Greetings: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of the Town of Hingham qualified to vote in Town affairs to meet at the Hingham High School, 17 Union Street, in said Hingham, on Thursday October 29, 2026 at 7:00 pm, then and there to act on the Warrant Articles listed below. You are hereby also directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of the Town of Hingham qualified to vote in Town affairs to meet at three designated polling places in said Town of Hingham according to their precinct, to wit: Precinct 1, 2, 3, and 4: High School, 17 Union Street; Precincts 5, 6, and 7: Middle School, 1103 Main Street; and Precinct 7A: Willard Square at Linden Ponds on Tuesday, November 3, 2026 from 7:00 am until 8:00 pm, then and there to give their votes on the official ballot for: to give their votes “Yes” or “No” on the following Town ballot questions: • Plymouth River Elementary School: Shall the Town of Hingham be allowed to exempt from the provisions of proposition two and one-half, so-called, the amounts required to pay for the bond issued in order to pay the costs of the roof system replacement, including the payment of all costs incidental or related thereto, at the Plymouth River Elementary School located at 200 High Street, Hingham, MA? • South Elementary School: Shall the Town of Hingham be allowed to exempt from the provisions of proposition two and one-half, so-called, the amounts required to pay for the bond issued in order to pay the costs of the roof system replacement, including the payment of all costs incidental or related thereto, at the South Elementary School located at 831 Main Street, Hingham, MA? Hereof fail not and make due return of this warrant with your doings thereon to the Town Clerk on or before October 1, 2026. Given under our hands at Hingham this twenty-ninth day of September 2026. Elizabeth F. Klein, Chair___ William C. Ramsey ___ Julie M. Strehle___ SELECT BOARD A true copy Attest: By virtue of the within warrant I hereby certify that I have noticed and warned the inhabitants of the Town of Hingham, qualified to vote in Town affairs to meet at the time and place indicated in the above warrant by causing a notice thereof to be published in The Hingham Journal fourteen days at least before the day appointed for said meeting. An attested copy was presented and posted by the Town Clerk in the Town Hall as of this date. ___ Horatio Hemmings Constable of Hingham October 1, 2026 4 ARTICLE 1 SOUTH ELEMENTARY SCHOOL ROOF Will the Town raise and appropriate, borrow or transfer from available funds, a sufficient sum of money to be expended under the direction of the 2025 School Building Committee for the roof system replacement, including the payment of all costs incidental or related thereto (the “Project”), at the South Elementary School located at 831 Main Street, Hingham, MA, which proposed repair Project would materially extend the useful life of the school and preserve an asset that otherwise is capable of supporting the required educational program, and for which the Town may be eligible for a school construction grant from the Massachusetts School Building Authority (“MSBA”). The Town acknowledges that the MSBA’s grant program is a non-entitlement, discretionary program based on need, as determined by the MSBA, and any Project costs the Town incurs in excess of any grant approved by and received from the MSBA shall be the sole responsibility of the Town. Any grant that the Town may receive from the MSBA for the Project shall not exceed the lesser (1) thirty six, and eighty-nine hundredths’ percent (36.89%) of eligible, approved Project costs, as determined by the MSBA, or (2) the total maximum grant amount determined by the MSBA, or act on anything relating thereto? (Inserted at the request of the 2025 School Building Committee) COMMENT: This Article seeks authorization to fund the replacement of the roof systems at South Elementary School (“South”). The existing roof systems are of varying ages and conditions and have required repairs and maintenance over time; much of the system has reached the end of its useful life. Recently, water infiltration from ice dams required an emergency response. The proposed Project is being developed in conjunction with the Massachusetts School Building Authority (“MSBA”) Accelerated Repair Program. Background South was constructed in 1948. The school roof is approximately 57,000 square feet. The building underwent an extensive expansion and renovation in 1998 at which point the school’s roofing systems were also completely replaced. Since that time the district has maintained it mainly through targeted repairs, with an emergency repair performed as recently as summer 2025. A 2022 study performed by Habeeb & Associates, the Town’s professional consultants, found that most of the 13 sections of the roofing (and the associated drainage fixtures) needed repair, and noted that the roof systems had exceeded their 20-year warranty. The report further noted that all roofing sections were approaching the end of their standard 25-year life expectancy and thus should be replaced in the near to intermediate term. As part of this roof Project Habeeb & Associates has been contracted to conduct a peer review of all design materials being submitted through the MSBA process. 2025 Annual Town Meeting authorized $320,000 for a schematic design study for the anticipated roofing systems replacement. The Town was subsequently accepted into the MSBA Accelerated Repair Program, and an Owner’s Project Manager was selected by the MSBA. All six public school buildings are actively required to accommodate current and projected student enrollment, based on Hingham Public Schools' facility evaluations and long-term planning. Overall enrollment is experiencing an increase, and over the next 10 years, elementary enrollments are projected by New England School Development Council (“NESDEC”) to increase by 304 students. 5 Building Study and Design Process To-Date Following the Town's acceptance into the MSBA's Accelerated Repair Program, the Project's design consultant, Gale Associates (“Gale”), was engaged to evaluate the roof and develop a schematic design. The April, 2026, evaluation included a visual assessment of the roofing and flashing; limited exploratory openings; hazardous-material sampling; an infrared drone survey; and a structural feasibility study. A related Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (“MAAB”) evaluation was subsequently conducted in early May, 2026. A whole roof system assessment study found that many portions of the South roof sub-structure are sound. Original timber framing installed in 1948, does not meet current snow-load Building Code (“Code”) requirements, and requires structural augmentation. In addition, several framing members in the 1998 expansion are very close to their maximum capacity (98%), and Gale recommended structural augmentation for that portion of the building as well. The remaining portions of the roof framing and decks are generally capable of supporting current code-required loads, although several framing members require reinforcement due to insufficient capacity for the additional load of future solar panels. Although the Town is not obligated to install solar panels, under the MSBA grant program, the roof structure must have a designated solar-ready area with sufficient capacity to support solar panels. The evaluation further found that most of the asphalt shingle and low-slope membrane roofing areas are more than 20 years old and showing signs of deterioration, including damaged shingles, poor-condition roof coatings, previous repairs related to water infiltration, and deteriorated flashing, sealants, and masonry. While the existing standing-seam metal roofing is generally serviceable, replacing it as part of the Project would provide a uniform, warrantable, and betterinsulated roof system. Limited hazardous-material testing found no asbestos in the samples collected, although additional testing will be required as the project progresses. Lead-based paint was identified on a roof truss, and the Project budget includes an allowance for potential abatement of both asbestos and lead. Lower-cost coating and overlay options for the existing roofing systems were also considered. These options were not recommended because they would not address the underlying deterioration and would require continued maintenance and repairs. The study concluded that continued patching and repairs would not provide a durable, long-term solution. The recommended approach is to replace the roof systems and address related flashing, masonry and drainage problems at the same time. Following Gale’s review, roof-covering options and cost comparisons were reviewed with Hingham Public Schools and the 2025 School Building Committee (“SBC”) in public meetings in June 2026. The SBC voted to proceed with PVC membrane roofing on the low-slope areas and standing-seam metal panels on the steep-slope areas. That direction, combined with findings on the age and condition of the existing systems, culminated in a Schematic Design submitted to the MSBA on August 27, 2026, and revised on September 18, 2026; this Schematic Design is the basis for the scope and cost estimate presented in this Article. Proposed Project The proposed Project will replace the existing roofing systems down to the roof decks, with the decks inspected and repaired as needed. The work will include new low-slope and steep-slope 6 roofing systems, along with related improvements to roof edges, flashing, drainage, gutters and downspouts, and rooftop equipment. The Project will also include reinforcement of selected roof framing and related interior work to meet current Code requirements and support potential future solar installation in the designated areas. Because the proposed roof assemblies will be thicker than the existing assemblies, related modifications will be required to drainage, roof-edge and flashing systems, as well as portions of the masonry. The work will also include masonry repairs, replacement of deteriorated sealants, and replacement or modification of existing roof ladders and other roof-access components. Because the Project cost exceeds 30% of the building’s assessed value, the Project must address accessibility throughout the building, not just in areas directly affected by the roof work. Thus, the Project will include accessibility improvements identified through a review of the school for compliance with applicable MAAB requirements. The preliminary scope includes modifications to toilet-room accessories, door hardware, portions of the exterior ramp and sidewalk, handrails, signage, vestibule flooring, doors and thresholds, and water coolers. Proposed Project Cost Based on the current Schematic Design, the total Project cost is $8,576,727, an increase from the $5,400,000 estimate presented at the 2025 Annual Town Meeting. The study and evaluation of the existing roof identified additional needs, most notably the augmentation of the wood-framed roof and structural steel trusses. The expanded scope was not contemplated in the previous estimate and has been incorporated into the current Project cost. Furthermore, Project costs have increased significantly over the past two years, reflecting continued construction cost escalation and broader inflationary pressures affecting labor and materials. Major cost elements include: Item / Category Estimated Cost Construction $7,064,575 Soft Costs (Feasibility, Admin, Design Fees, etc.) $1,123,600 Contingencies (Construction & Owner Project Manager) $ 388,552 Total Project Budget $8,576,727 The Project may not exceed the authorized amount without further authorization by Town Meeting. Final design development, MSBA review, and construction bidding will occur within this authorized Project budget. Financing This Project is being pursued through the MSBA Accelerated Repair Program, which is a nonentitlement, discretionary program. Reimbursement is based on eligible and approved Project costs. In accordance with MSBA requirements, this Article seeks authorization for the full Project cost of up to $8,576,727. The maximum MSBA grant is 36.89% of eligible, approved Project costs. Eligible, approved costs are presently estimated to be $7,787,441, resulting in an estimated 7 MSBA reimbursement of $2,872,787. The projected Town share would be approximately $5,703,940. This would be funded through excluded debt, which is exempt from the property tax cap under Proposition 2½. Excluded debt requires a 2/3 vote of Town Meeting and a majority ballot vote for adoption. If this Article is approved, the associated excluded debt service would result in an estimated FY28 property tax increase of approximately $55 for the average assessed-value home ($1,367,000) in addition to the annual property tax increase allowed under Proposition 2½. Hours Contact Search FY27 Budget Info/Schedule October 2026 Town Meeting Warrant - Text Home Committees Finance Committee October 2026 Town Meeting Warrant - Text October 2026 Town Meeting Warrant - Text In the name of the Commonwealth you are hereby required to notify and warn the inhabitants of the Town of Holliston who are qualified to vote in Town Affairs to meet in the Holliston High School Auditorium, 370 Hollis Street, Holliston, MA: MONDAY, OCTOBER 19, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. to act on the following Articles, to wit: ARTICLE 1: GENERAL STABILIZATION FUND SPONSORED BY: Select Board ESTIMATED COST: $150,000 To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds a sum of money for the General Stabilization Fund; or take any action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: The balance of the General Stabilization Fund as of July 1, 2026 is $10.96 million. With no planned use within the Warrant below, the projected ending balance of the fund after October l Town Meeting would be $11.11 million, or 14.49% of the FY27 budgeted expenditures. This Article ensures that the balance of the General Stabilization Fund stays within range of the Town’s Financial Policies as updated in September 2024, specifically moving funds to stay above the target of 12% of General Fund Expenditures, but below the maximum ratio of 18%. ($150,000 from Free Cash) THE FINANCE COMMITTEE RECOMMENDS THAT THE TOWN APPROPRIATE $150,000 FROM FREE CASH TO THE GENERAL STABILIZATION FUND (UNANIMOUS) ARTICLE 2: PENSION STABILIZATION FUND SPONSORED BY: Select Board ESTIMATED COST: $250,000 To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds a sum of money for the Pension Stabilization Fund; or take any action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: The May 2021 Annual Town Meeting established a fund to address the unfunded liability associated with pensions of municipal employees. State statute dictates that pension systems must be fully funded by 2040, and both the Middlesex County Retirement System (MCRS) and the Massachusetts Teachers Retirement System (MTRS) are approximately 60% funded. The Fund will allow the Town to address its unfunded liability while continuing to meet its current obligations. Should the legally required contributions to MCRS increase significantly in future years, this fund can also be used to protect the Town from negative budget impacts related to meeting this obligation. With an estimated fiscal year starting balance of $1.92 million, this appropriation would bring the balance to approximately $2.17 million, invested with the State’s PRIT system, consistent with the Town’s OPEB Trust Fund. ($250,000 from Free Cash) THE FINANCE COMMITTEE RECOMMENDS THAT THE TOWN APPROPRIATE $250,000 FROM FREE CASH TO THE PENSION STABILIZATION FUND (UNANIMOUS) ARTICLE 3: CAPITAL EXPENDITURE FUND SPONSORED BY: Select Board ESTIMATED COST: $2,100,000 To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds a sum of money for the Capital Expenditure Fund; or take any action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: The Capital Expenditure Fund (CapEx) is used to fund capital expenses. An illustrative example of those capital expenses can be found under the Capital Budget (Article 11) in this Warrant. If all capital items utilizing CapEx funding in Articles 11 are approved, as presented in the warrant, the fund balance will be approximately $1.60 M million after October Town Meeting – assuming at least $2.1 million in Free Cash is available for appropriation by this article. This is the working estimate the Town has used for preparation for the Fall Town Meeting. The balance cannot be drawn down below $1.5 million or the Town would be at risk of conflicting with the Financial Policies (Min. Balance is 2% of Operating Expenditures). Article 11 below is the only proposed use of CapEx funding in October 2025. (Estimated $2,100,000 from Free Cash, pending final certification of Free Cash by the Department of Revenue) THE FINANCE COMMITTEE RECOMMENDS THAT THE TOWN APPROPRIATE $2,309,670 FROM FREE CASH AND $1,000,000 FROM ARTICLE 19 OF THE AY 2025 TOWN MEETING TO THE CAPITAL EXPENDITURE FUND (UNANIMOUS) ARTICLE 4: CLASSIFICATION PLAN: POSITION TITLE CHANGES SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend the job classification plan for full and part-time employees effective July 1, 2026 as approved at the May 2026 Annual Town Meeting by adding the following position title: POSITION PROPOSED GRADE Permitting Coordinator 400 ,or take any other action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: The addition of this job title allows the town’s Planning Department to change the job title of the Administrative Clerk that supports the department to “Planning Coordinator.” The Administrative Clerk was also approved at a Grade 400 at the May 2026 Annual Town Meeting, so there is no financial impact or additional resources needed to make this change. This change would be part of a larger effort to better define the responsibilities of the role ARTICLE 5: PERSONNEL BYLAW AMENDMENT: DEFINITIONS SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 3 of the Consolidated Personnel By-Law by inserting the following definition after Holiday Pay: Immediate Family: The immediate family shall consist of the employee’s father, mother, relative residing in the same household, father-in-law, mother-in-law, sister, brother, spouse, child, grandparents, and grandchildren. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: This amendment adds a definition of immediate family to the Personnel Bylaw, which mirrors the definition included in collective bargaining agreements. ARTICLE 6: PERSONNEL BYLAW AMENDMENT: SORI REQUIREMENTS SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 6 of the Consolidated Personnel By-Law to read as follows: SECTION 6: BACKGROUND CHECK For the mutual protection of the Town and its employees, successful candidates for employment, as the Town Administrator may require, shall be subject to a background check, which may include, but not be limited to, a criminal history background check (C.O.R.I.) and/or a sexual offender history check (S.O.R.I.). The Town Administrator shall review the background check to determine, in their discretion, whether it impacts the decision to employ the candidate. , or take any other action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: This proposed amendment to the personnel by-law allows for the Town to run SORI checks for individuals seeking employment in positions with potential unmonitored contact with vulnerable populations. This practice modernization is aimed at protecting residents and the Town. ARTICLE 7: PERSONNEL BYLAW AMENDMENT: VACATION ACCRUALS SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend Sections 9, 10, and 11 of the Consolidated Personnel By-Law to read as follows: (deleted language shown in strikethrough and new language underlined): SECTION 9: VACATION POLICY Vacation leave may be taken when it is accrued, for a given fiscal year may be taken at any time during the fiscal year subject to the approval of the department head or other appropriate authority. Ten days two weeks of vacation leave may be carried over from one fiscal year to another, with the approval of the Town Administrator. Vacation leave with pay shall not be granted to temporary, on-call or seasonal employees. SECTION 10: VACATION LEAVE FOR FULL-TIME PERMANENT EMPLOYEES Vacation leave shall be granted to full-time permanent employees as follows: a. Effective July 1, 2027, vacation leave will accrue monthly, beginning on an employee’s date of hire, based on service completed during the previous month. of one (1) week with full pay shall be granted to any employee who has been employed by the town for at least six (6) full calendar months as of the first day of July following the employee’s date of hire. Employees with less than six (6) full calendar months of employment as of July 1 following their date of hire will be credited with a prorated amount of the one week of vacation time on that July 1. b. Vacation leave of two (2) weeks per year with full pay will accrue monthly for employees with 0 – 5 years of service. shall be granted to any employee who has been employed by the town for twelve (12) full calendar months as of July 1 of a given year. c. Vacation leave of three (3) weeks per year with full pay will accrue monthly for employees with 6 – 10 years of service. shall be granted to any employee who has been employed by the town for five (5) full years as of July 1 of a given year. d. Vacation leave of four (4) weeks per year with full pay will accrue monthly for employees with 11 – 15 years of service. shall be granted to any employee who has been employed by the town for twenty (20) full years as of July 1 of a given year. e. Vacation leave of five (5) weeks per year with full pay will accrue monthly for employees with 16 or more years of service. shall be granted to any employee who has been employed by the town for twenty (20) full years as of July 1 of a given year. f. Full pay, as used in this section, refers to the employee's regular straight-time salary or wages based on the rate paid at the time vacation pay is drawn. g. Vacation leave provided on July 1 of a given year is earned on a prorated monthly basis during the previous Fiscal Year. Employees who separate from Town employment will receive payment for any unused but accrued earned vacation leave. h. No more than 10 days (2 weeks) of vacation leave may be carried over from one year to the next. SECTION 11: VACATION LEAVE FOR PART-TIME EMPLOYEES Part-time permanent employees shall be entitled to prorated vacation leave based on the ratio of their part-time employment to full-time employment within their department. Vacation credited as of July 1 will be based upon the number of hours worked the previous fiscal year. , or take any other action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: These proposed amendments seek to update current vacation policies that are out of date and not competitive. Under the “annual accrual” process currently in place, an employee hired in July would not receive their two weeks of vacation time until after the first year of employment. This has resulted in the Town losing highly qualified candidates in recent months. ARTICLE 8: PERSONNEL BYLAW AMENDMENT: PERSONAL TIME ACCRUALS SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 12 of the Consolidated Personnel By-Law to read as follows: (deleted language in strikethrough and proposed new language underlined: SECTION 12: LEAVES OF ABSENCE Leaves of absence may be granted to permanent employees during a calendar year subject to the following provisions: a. Three two (2) days leave of absence with full pay shall be granted to permanent employees for personal business during any fiscal calendar year with written approval of the department head, and shall be requested at least twenty-four (24) hours prior to the date selected. Effective January 1, 2027, all permanent employees will be credited with 1.5 personal days, and then with 3 personal days on July 1, 2027, and on every July 1 thereafter. Personal time must be used by the end of the fiscal year it is earned and cannot be carried over. b. Except as otherwise provided in this By-Law, all other leaves of absence shall be without compensation and shall be subject to the written approval of the department head and Town Administrator, c. Permanent employees are allowed to take up to six (6) days leave with pay during any calendar year to attend to illness in the employee's immediate family. Such leave shall be deducted from the employee's sick leave. d. Statutory and certain other types of leaves of absence can be found in the Town’s Personnel Policies (See Town Website for Policies). , or take any other action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: This proposed amendment has two objectives. First, it would grant personal days on a fiscal year basis, as opposed to on a calendar year basis. This would bring personal time in line with the way the Town grants vacation and sick time for eligible employees. The proposal also increases the personal days granted annually to eligible employees from two days to three days, which is comparable to nearby municipalities. ARTICLE 9: PERSONNEL BYLAW AMENDMENT: SICK & BEREAVEMENT LEAVE SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 17 of the Consolidated Personnel By-Law to read as follows (deleted language in strikethrough and proposed new language underlined: SECTION 17 BEREAVEMENT LEAVE Bereavement leave with full pay, not to exceed five (5) days, in the discretion of the employee’s department head, may be granted to any permanent employee for a death in the employee’s immediate family. For purposes of this section, the immediate family shall consist of the employee’s father, mother, domestic partner, significant other residing in the same household, father-in-law, mother-in-law, sister, brother, spouse, child, grandparents and grandchildren. For the purposes of this section, the immediate family shall consist of the employee’s father, mother, relative residing in the same household, father-in-law, mother-in-law, sister, brother, spouse, child, grandparents, and grandchildren. This section shall also apply to parents who suffer loss of pregnancy. , or take any other action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: This article would update Section 17 of the Personnel Bylaw with the language proposed in Article 6, while also adding language allowing for bereavement to be granted to parents suffering loss of pregnancy. ARTICLE 10: PERSONNEL BYLAW AMENDMENT: TOWN MANAGER ACT SPONSORED BY: Select Board To see if the Town will vote to amend the Consolidated Personnel By-Law to reflect the passage of the Town Manager Act both by the Massachusetts General Court and the Holliston October 2024 Town Meeting, by changing any references to “Town Administrator” to “Town Manager” and updating the position description for consistency therewith, or take any other action relative thereto. SELECT BOARD COMMENTS: This amendment simply updates the pertinent section and other references to the Town Administrator in the Personnel By-law to reflect the adoption of the Town Manager Act. As referenced in the comments of Article 3, if Article 3 passes as written and all remaining of the items proposed to be funding out of the Capital Expenditure Fund are approved in Article 11, the remaining balance of the fund will be $1,602,433 – assuming an estimated deposit into the fund of $2,100,000 pending Free Cash certification. The $100,000 proposed appropriation from the Water Enterprise Retained Earnings is for the purposes of maintaining compliance with the EPAs' Lead Service Line Compliance Plan. The plan requires that all water services connected to the Holliston water system be physically verified to be absent of lead and/or galvanized steel. If present, service connections require replacement. This requires physical excavations of the service at the town curb stop. To date the Town has completed 50 excavations. There are 3038 public side services requiring excavation with a total 5018 total connected services. This is an on-going project with the next EPA milestone deadline of November 1, 2027 with the deliverable of a baseline inventory and the lead service line plan. Additional appropriations will be sought to complete the work and meet the EPA’s timeframe.
